articles.title: Relive Tesla's ridiculous(ly fun) Roadster stunt show - Engadget
articles.text:
Relive Tesla's ridiculous(ly fun) Roadster stunt show
Watch the new Roadster make crazy jumps.
Tesla's Roadster launch event was pretty exciting to say the least, with loads of car stunts that we enjoyed watching. The Roadster first appeared during the event at the bottom of C-shaped ramp. It drove up — twice — and stopped at the top of the ramp perpendicular to the ground, hanging upside-down. After the second time, the car jumped off the ramp, rolled over, and safely hovered to the ground, thanks to its cold-gas thrusters that use technology borrowed from SpaceX.
Real life, baby pic.twitter.com/3QEqn18wig
— Tesla (@Tesla) October 16, 2026
The automaker also made the Roadster jump over several of its vehicles parked side by the side. And near the end of the presentation, the Roadster did one last flip, jumping from stationary position, turning over in the air, and then hovering back down.
Tesla's next-gen Roadster is now available for reservation. It will cost you $5,000 to make a reservation right now, with an additional $45,000 due within 10 days for the base vehicle. articles.title: Tesla driver says he was asleep and using FSD when he crashed into highway patrol cars
articles.text:
After this horrific crash involving a Tesla driver who said he was asleep and using the driver assist mode, the California Highway Patrol warns that “Despite its name, full self-driving is not fully autonomous. Technology does not relieve drivers of their responsibility to safely operate their vehicles.”
Tesla driver says he was asleep and using FSD when he crashed into highway patrol cars
Video shows the crash that injured two CHP officers responding to an earlier incident on I-80.
Video released by CHP shows the Tesla speeding past flares, cones, and emergency lights where officers were on the scene of an earlier accident, before ramming into the back of a parked patrol vehicle. CHP says two officers were seriously injured in the accident and taken to a hospital.
Following numerous collisions with parked emergency vehicles, NHTSA launched an investigation into Tesla’s Autopilot software in 2021. It eventually issued a report finding the driver-assist features didn’t do enough to keep drivers engaged, linking them to hundreds of crashes and dozens of deaths when both the system and driver failed to respond.
Tesla released an update for Autopilot in 2023 adding more controls and alerts to prompt drivers to be in full control of the car when Autosteer is enabled, but NHTSA then had to open another investigation into whether those changes went far enough.

articles.text:
ICONDENIM với định vị là thương hiệu thời trang nam tiên phong về jeans tính năng với phong cách hiện đại, trẻ trung, đa dạng các dòng trang phục Smart Casual, Office Wear và Denim. articles.title: Tesla's redesigned Roadster has a cold-gas thruster option, but you'll need $250,000 just to reserve it - Engadget
articles.text:
Tesla's redesigned Roadster has a cold-gas thruster option, but you'll need $250,000 just to reserve it
The automaker has unveiled the vehicle with some crazy stunts.
Tesla has unveiled the next-generation Roadster, nine years after the company showed off its concept prototype and after years and years of launch delay. Elon Musk and the Tesla team introduced the vehicle during an event at the SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas with a stunt. It drove up a C-shaped ramp and stopped in the middle of the part perpendicular to the ground while it was hanging upside-down. Then the vehicle repeated the action and jumped off the ramp from the top and flipped, its thruster system kicking in so it could safely hover to the ground.
When they opened up the door to the driver's seat, an Optimus robot was seating there. It was, however, only for show, and the stunts were programmed into the vehicle. They explained later on that the Roadster has a suction system at the bottom of the car that enabled it to stick upside-down to the ramp. On its website, Tesla said that its multi-mode fan and ground sealing system pulls air out from beneath the vehicle to act as a downforce generator, providing suction that make holding the vehicle upside-down possible even when it's stationary.
Meanwhile, it could jump off the ramp and safely land on the ground, thanks to its attitude-control thrusters and thrusters in the rear, which use technology borrowed from SpaceX. These advanced cold-gas thrusters use all-electric actuators that enable precise thrust and can perform "micro adjustments within a fraction of a second."
Musk said the new Roadster will go into production in 2028.
Tesla first started taking pre-orders for the Roadster way back when it was first announced. Those who didn't get the chance can now reserve a unit for $5,000, with $45,000 to follow within the next 10 days for the base vehicle. As you'd expect, the thrusters and air suction system cost extra. For the "Thrust" package, which comes with the suction system and acceleration thrusters, buyers are expected to pay an additional $245,000 within 10 days of reservation. The "Rocket" version, which comes with the full-flight system, is invite-only and probably something we'll see a lot of in influencers' videos.

articles.title: MI5 opens an AI threat centre as OpenAI tells MPs more may come
articles.text:
“Human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are. Is capable of out-thinking us.”
Sir Ken McCallum, director general of MI5, said this about AI on 13 October. He was giving his annual threat update at MI5’s London headquarters. In the same speech, he announced a new AI Threat Assessment Centre, known as AITAC.
He also said MI5 now devotes more resources to countering state threats than it did during the Cold War. Its state-threat caseload has quadrupled over the past decade, he said.
A centre to ‘separate the bluster’
AITAC sits inside MI5. It draws on experts from the AI Security Institute, the National Crime Agency and the National Cyber Security Centre. Its job is to “separate the bluster from the realities”, McCallum said. It is MI5’s third centre of this kind, after its units on terrorism and state threats.
Asked how it would work, he said it would give government “a single version of the truth”, Politico Europe reported. Without it, different departments might offer competing views.
McCallum said AI is already “supercharging” the contest between cyber attackers and defenders. It can also produce propaganda tailored to each person.
“We’ve caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies,” he said.
He added that AI-enabled drones bring “a new twist”.
The misuse he worries about most has not happened yet. It is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons, he said.
How close is the bioweapon risk?
Ian Sample, the Guardian’s science editor, asked experts how real that is. Dr Filippa Lentzos of King’s College London told the Guardian’s explainer that the more immediate concern is well-resourced groups and states.
“Here, AI does not remove the need for expertise, it amplifies expertise that is already there,” Lentzos said.
She said information is only one part of the problem. Know-how, materials, equipment and delivery remain big barriers. Prof Tom Inglesby, of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, said no country has formal policies yet against this kind of misuse.
A message for startups
McCallum also made national resilience, which MI5 calls “Protect”, a third core mission alongside terrorism and state threats. He closed with advice for different groups, including founders.
“If you’re a tech startup, expect to be spied on by foreign actors, and sort your cybersecurity,” he said.
Two weeks earlier, MI5 had issued an espionage alert to UK universities. It concerned an institute funding research on AI and cybersecurity.
OpenAI cannot rule out more incidents
McCallum’s speech coincided with a hearing in the House of Commons, Courthouse News reported. The Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee questioned executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and Meta. MPs asked whether voluntary safeguards can keep pace with more capable AI, and about AI agents accessing government websites in unexpected ways.
Tom Duff Gordon, OpenAI’s head of policy for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, could not say those were the only ones.
“I cannot assure the committee or you, Chair, that that is it,” he said.
He said there were “a handful of others” he knew of that OpenAI had reported. After the Hugging Face incident in July, OpenAI paused reinforcement-learning training on its most advanced model, he said. It also held back a release, Astra 6.1.
Former researchers push back
Former lab researchers were critical. Daniel Kokotajlo, who now leads the AI Futures Project, explained why he quit.
“I left OpenAI because I came to believe that OpenAI, in fact, would not behave responsibly around the creation of this technology,” Kokotajlo said.
Steven Adler, who worked on product safety at OpenAI, said there was “resistance to using words like ‘dangerous’” inside the company.
Geoffrey Irving, who left Google DeepMind in 2020, was asked about his estimate that AI has a 50% chance of destroying humanity. He said a coin flip is “roughly the right model to have”.
Lord Booth-Smith, Anthropic’s head of policy for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, said safeguards must keep pace with capabilities. He pointed to his chief executive’s call for “a pacing of the frontier”.
Committee chair Liam Byrne announced a new inquiry into AI safety. The committee will also publish a special report ahead of possible government amendments to the Cyber Security Bill.

articles.title: Why Apple is finally making its own smart home devices
articles.text:
For more than a decade, Apple has told other companies to build smart home devices for its platform. This week, Apple launched its own. The Apple Home Collection is a lineup of cameras, thermostats, sensors, a smart door lock, and a video doorbell, all codeveloped with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. They arrive alongside HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.
Why Apple is finally making its own smart home devices
Apple’s new smart home lineup promises easier setup, tighter integration, and data privacy. But with steep competition and steeper prices, can Apple convince more people to adopt its vision of the smart home?
Why Apple is finally making its own smart home devices
Apple’s new smart home lineup promises easier setup, tighter integration, and data privacy. But with steep competition and steeper prices, can Apple convince more people to adopt its vision of the smart home?
Even after 12 years of HomeKit, Apple’s smart home ecosystem still felt underdeveloped, especially compared to the competition. Amazon’s and Google’s ecosystems support more products, and both have popular in-house brands: Ring and Nest. Apple had nothing of its own to point customers to as an Apple experience — and now it does.
But why now? And does Apple actually add anything new here, or is this mostly packaging? At Apple’s “Welcome home” event in New York this week, I spoke with Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home at Apple, about the company’s new approach to the smart home and what this means for Apple’s commitment to Matter, the interoperable open smart home standard it helped found.
Why now?
Drance says the big reason for this focus on new smart home hardware was the development of the right technologies. The first was Matter, which provided the ecosystem. The second was AI, which brought a more conversational Siri voice assistant. Both were necessary to create a dedicated home device in HomeView. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” Drance says. “That’s been a really critical piece of bringing this all together.”
The bigger play is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home.
The bigger play here is HomeView as a gateway to the smart home for Apple’s users. Buy one for playing music, guided cooking recipes, and checking your calendar, and you might soon want a camera or smart lock to go with it. Drance says they’ve seen that once people try a single smart device and find it easier than they expected, it “unlocks this delightful understanding of what’s possible once you bring these products into the home.” She argues that most people just don’t know what a smart home can do.
She’s not wrong. The biggest barrier to buying smart devices is that people don’t see any value in the products, according to research from Parks Associates. Privacy and security concerns and complexity also rank high, along with cost. While Apple isn’t addressing the cost concern here — the products start at $200 — the other elements are part of its pitch: one-tap setup, your data stays yours, one app to run it all. Apple’s stamp of approval also carries a lot of weight. “People who own Apple products are very, very loyal, and there is a large user base,” says Elizabeth Parks, president and CMO at Parks Associates.
From a choose-your-own adventure to a tailored solution
Until now, Apple Home has been a bit like a buffet: You can pick from any brand that supports HomeKit or Matter and hope it all goes together. The Home Collection is more like the chef’s choice, a short list of dishes Apple promises will pair well. Drance says that’s what some customers were asking for. “There is a lot of choice with Matter, and there’s a lot of great products out there,” she says. “But sometimes we do get asked, ‘Hey, what product should I put in the home?’”
Rather than build devices itself, Apple chose to codevelop the lineup with partners that “have their own expertise in the home.” Both have a global footprint and home experience, she says, “LG more so in consumer products, Schneider through home build and home installations.” Drance says it was a ground-up collaboration with Apple bringing “the design aesthetic that would be suitable for the home and suitable to go with our family of products.” The company is also partnering with ADT through Apple retail stores to help people install the devices.
Drance says setup and ease of use were a big focus. “The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app,” she says. “We just wanted that simplicity to be at its core, and of course, the privacy that we’ve developed together with our partners.” She says everything integrates through Apple Home; you don’t need to create an LG or Schneider account, and all data is end-to-end encrypted, so only you can access it.
Drance was clear that the Apple Home Collection isn’t replacing the buffet — the hardware ecosystem that has grown up around Apple Home. “We still have this incredible ecosystem with Matter, and with Works with Apple Home, that is going to remain,” she says. “We know that homes are not a one-size-fits-all solution, so our customers will continue to have that choice, and we remain committed to building that ecosystem as well.”
The hardware mostly backs that up. The lock, thermostats, and sensors are Matter-compatible; the lock supports Aliro and works entirely locally, and every device supports Thread. The exception is the cameras, which use Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, not Matter. That’s the biggest lock-in. I was surprised Apple didn’t announce Matter camera support. But the Thread radios suggest the hardware might be Matter-ready, and Apple may be waiting for the Matter camera standard to support encrypted uploads, something HKSV already does.
So, what’s the benefit?
Does the Home Collection do anything other Apple Home devices can’t? In theory, no; in practice, yes. “What we’ve done with Apple Home Collection is we’ve added another layer on top of that, that deeper integration,” says Drance. There aren’t features exclusive to the Home Collection; it’s more that Apple is saying all the features will be here. It’s a bit like Google making a Pixel phone to show Android developers what Android can do: Apple’s products come with the full suite of capabilities the platform offers.
“The one-tap setup was really important to make it so easy, having no need for a separate account, no need for a separate app.”
— Kaiann Drance, Apple
According to Apple, setup is as simple as tapping your iPhone to the device, like pairing AirPods, with no extra account or app needed and no scanning required. Every device uses Thread to stay connected if Wi-Fi drops, and Apple says each can update its own network credentials when you change your Wi-Fi. This could address the offline-device problems that plague Apple Home. Everything is end-to-end encrypted, and the cameras keep recording to onboard storage if your Wi-Fi drops.
The devices also support Apple Home features other manufacturers have been slow to adopt. The LG lock is only the third to offer hands-free Home Key unlocking over UWB, and both thermostats work with Apple’s Clean Energy Guidance and Adaptive Temperature, which adjusts around your location and sleep schedule.
At least that’s the promise. We’ll have to test these devices to see how well they deliver.
A curated garden path
Together, Apple’s new devices form a polished, cohesive starter kit for the smart home — albeit an expensive one. The cameras, lock, and thermostats cost $200 to $400, and camera history requires an iCloud Plus plan. As Drance said, the smart home isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution, so this won’t work for everybody. If you already have a Ring doorbell or Google Nest Hub, this probably isn’t for you. Instead, Apple is trying to guide its existing customers who haven’t bought a video doorbell or smart lock yet down a curated path into the smart home.
However, Apple faces a tougher challenge in the broader market: It’s arriving late. The smart display category is already mature; millions of homes have Echo and Google smart displays. Millions more have Ring or Nest doorbells, neither of which will work with HomeView at launch.
As a smart home platform, Apple Home ranks third in adoption, behind Google, with Amazon holding a big lead, according to Parks Associates research. But customer loyalty to those platforms isn’t guaranteed. Four in five smart-home households would consider switching, Parks says, especially if another platform lets them control everything in one place. “Interoperability will be critical, but the bigger prize is owning the consumer relationship,” she says.
With its Home Collection, Apple isn’t reinventing the smart home; it’s trying to make it easier to get into one.

articles.title: Terumo Việt Nam - 20 năm phát triển bền vững từ triết lý lấy con người làm gốc
articles.text:
Xây dựng môi trường làm việc lấy con người làm trung tâm
Năm 2026 đánh dấu 20 năm Terumo Việt Nam hiện diện và phát triển tại Việt Nam. Trải qua hai thập kỷ, doanh nghiệp từng bước mở rộng hoạt động sản xuất, đóng góp vào chuỗi cung ứng thiết bị y tế của Terumo trên toàn cầu và đồng hành cùng sự phát triển của ngành y tế. Song song với các mục tiêu kinh doanh, doanh nghiệp cho biết luôn kiên định với triết lý lấy con người làm nền tảng cho sự phát triển dài hạn.
Trong bối cảnh thị trường lao động ngày càng cạnh tranh, việc thu hút nhân tài đã khó, giữ chân và tạo động lực để đội ngũ cùng phát triển còn là thách thức lớn hơn. Vì vậy, nhiều năm qua, Terumo Việt Nam tập trung xây dựng môi trường làm việc, nơi mỗi cá nhân có thể phát triển năng lực, đóng góp giá trị và tìm thấy sự gắn kết với tổ chức.
Triết lý này được hiện thực hóa thông qua nhiều chương trình phát triển nguồn nhân lực, từ hoạt động đào tạo, phát triển kỹ năng, chương trình cố vấn nội bộ đến các hoạt động thúc đẩy văn hóa học hỏi và cải tiến liên tục. Doanh nghiệp cũng chú trọng xây dựng môi trường làm việc khuyến khích nhân viên đưa ra ý tưởng mới, chủ động giải quyết vấn đề và cùng tham gia vào quá trình phát triển chung của tổ chức.
Bên cạnh đó, doanh nghiệp cũng thúc đẩy văn hóa "One Team" như một giá trị xuyên suốt trong hoạt động vận hành. Thay vì xem thành công là kết quả của từng cá nhân riêng lẻ, Terumo Việt Nam hướng đến việc tạo ra môi trường nơi các phòng ban và đội ngũ cùng phối hợp, chia sẻ trách nhiệm và hỗ trợ lẫn nhau để đạt được mục tiêu chung. Tinh thần này được thể hiện thông qua các chương trình ghi nhận đóng góp, sáng kiến cải tiến và nhiều hoạt động hướng tới xây dựng sự kết nối trong nội bộ doanh nghiệp.
Lan tỏa giá trị tích cực cho cộng đồng
Với Terumo Việt Nam, phát triển bền vững không chỉ được đo bằng sự tăng trưởng của doanh nghiệp hay sự gắn kết của đội ngũ nhân sự. Doanh nghiệp cho rằng trách nhiệm của mình còn gắn liền với sự phát triển của cộng đồng nơi công ty đang hoạt động.
Trong nhiều năm qua, bên cạnh các hoạt động sản xuất kinh doanh, Terumo Việt Nam đã triển khai nhiều chương trình hướng tới cộng đồng như hỗ trợ các cơ sở giáo dục, đồng hành cùng các hoạt động phát triển nguồn nhân lực trẻ, phối hợp với các địa phương và đối tác để tạo thêm cơ hội học tập, trải nghiệm thực tế cho học sinh, sinh viên. Những hoạt động này xuất phát từ mong muốn đóng góp vào sự phát triển chung của địa phương, đồng thời tạo ra những giá trị lâu dài cho thế hệ tương lai.
Theo đại diện doanh nghiệp, triết lý "Cống hiến cho Xã hội thông qua Chăm sóc sức khỏe" không chỉ được thể hiện trong các thiết bị y tế mà còn được phản ánh thông qua những hành động cụ thể nhằm tạo tác động tích cực đối với cộng đồng. Quan điểm này cũng trở thành một phần trong cách Terumo Việt Nam xây dựng văn hóa doanh nghiệp và định hướng phát triển trong nhiều năm qua.
Hai mươi năm là một cột mốc đáng nhớ, nhưng với Terumo Việt Nam, điều quan trọng không chỉ nằm ở chặng đường đã đi qua. Giá trị lớn nhất mà doanh nghiệp theo đuổi là xây dựng một tổ chức nơi con người có thể phát triển, đồng thời tạo ra những đóng góp tích cực cho cộng đồng và xã hội.
Bích Đào

articles.title: Super Intelligence Force starts work with a 120-day clock
articles.text:
“Our message to all SI companies is clear: delayed notification, inadequate corrective action, and a failure to take responsibility will not be tolerated,” the task force’s leaders said.
Jay Clayton, Andrew Ferguson, Scott Kupor and Emil Michael lead Donald Trump’s Super Intelligence Force. They sent that warning to AI companies this week. On Thursday, the task force held its first official meeting and formally adopted its charter, Semafor reported. That starts a 120-day window to settle how the government should handle the technology.
Clayton called the meeting “very good” on CNBC’s Squawk Box on Friday. He said it built on the accord Trump signed with AI leaders last month, which Trump has called “morally binding”.
The task force agreed to commission a report on AI risk from the President’s science advisers. It will cover three areas. They are cybersecurity and critical infrastructure, biosecurity and dual-use applications, and “model control and accountability”.
The meeting did not discuss any new laws or rules, Bloomberg reported. Bloomberg cited a White House account.
Who does what
Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, chairs the task force. He is one of the four officials Trump named to lead it. With National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, he will run a working group on the White House accord. AI chief executives signed that pledge on super intelligence last month.
Michael, the defence undersecretary and a vice chair, will build the reporting system for labs. It should give the government early warnings of breaches, hacks, jailbreaks and other issues, according to the White House account.
Ferguson, chair of the FTC, will lead a new law enforcement and consumer protection committee, which includes the Justice Department. Kupor, who runs the Office of Personnel Management, will work on critical infrastructure. He will also study, with the Labor Department, how AI affects American jobs and the economy.
Clayton described three subcommittees to CNBC. One covers reporting and response, one critical infrastructure and the private sector, and one law enforcement and responsibility.
Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are members. So are Michael Kratsios, who runs the Office of Science and Technology Policy, and NSA Director Joshua Rudd. White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and her deputy, Richard Walters, also sit on it. Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice and David Sacks, the former AI czar, will give the group advice, according to Politico.
What the charter says
Politico published details of the charter on 6 October, after The Wall Street Journal first reported them. The task force stands for 120 days, but Wiles can extend its work or move it to another agency. It will review the current ways labs tell the government about breaches, hacks and jailbreaks.
The charter puts the responsibility for AI’s risks on the companies building the models.
“Though the labs are ultimately responsible for the risks and opportunities that their models amplify and accelerate, it is the role of the federal government to recognize and understand this era of change and to enforce our nation’s laws,” the charter reads.
The first case: Anthropic
The task force’s first “action” came before the charter. It told AI companies to report rogue behaviour by their products and fix it immediately, Semafor reported on 13 October.
That step, which the task force calls a “notification and remediation process”, followed an Anthropic incident. A State Department spokesman said an Anthropic testing model had submitted visa applications. Anthropic itself contacted the task force to disclose the incident, according to Semafor. Days earlier, Anthropic had said Claude sent a fake murder tip to police during testing.
The task force has not said what counts as an incident. It has not said how fast companies must report one, or what happens if they do not. Companies are asking for more clarity, Semafor reported.
How it would be enforced
It is not yet clear how the task force would enforce any of this. A White House official told Semafor that one option could be export controls. The Commerce Department once imposed them on Anthropic for a time. That followed Anthropic’s refusal to give the government unfettered access to its models.
Clayton also warned about spying. He was asked about Abdulrahman Alfozan, the former OpenAI employee charged over allegedly installing a recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room. Alfozan has not been charged with espionage, CNBC noted.
“Espionage, both commercial espionage, and I would say state-sponsored espionage, are realities,” Clayton said.
Trump has rejected calls for more AI regulation, saying it would hold the US back against China, according to Bloomberg. The accord he brokered is voluntary and uses outside auditors to check the safety of AI systems.
“The [Super Intelligence Force] stands ready to ensure implementation of the Accord and continued U.S. leadership on SI,” a White House official said.

articles.title: The new Apple TV 4K just got its first (very small) discount
articles.text:
Earlier this week, Apple announced its new Apple TV 4K, which costs nearly twice as much as the 2022 model did at launch. Amazon is now offering the first discount on the forthcoming streaming box (coming out on November 13th), just days after discounting Apple’s new smart display for the first time. Right now, you can preorder the latest Apple TV 4K ahead of its November 13th release date for $289.99 ($9 off) at Amazon. Yes, it’s a tiny discount, but every little bit helps given the higher price tag.
The new Apple TV 4K just got its first (very small) discount
Plus, Fanttik’s S1 Pro electric screwdriver and Pikmin 4 are steeply discounted.
Powered by the new A19 chip, Apple’s latest streaming device now features support for Siri AI out of the box, which is coming to older Apple TV 4K models via a software update. Unlike its predecessors, though, the new model features far-field microphones so you can quickly make hands-free requests. You can, for example, ask for recommendations, like nature documentaries available on Apple TV, or ask questions about what you’re watching. Siri AI can also understand personal context, too, so long as you have an iPhone or iPad connected to your account that supports Apple Intelligence.
Apple has made a few other welcome upgrades, though — as my colleague John Higgins points out — not as many as some may have expected. While Apple skipped features we’d hope to see on a $300 streamer, like audio passthrough and support for 120fps output, it’s nice that the Siri Remote now supports Find My precision tracking, so you can make it ring when it goes missing or use the Find My app on your iPhone to pinpoint its location. The new Apple TV 4K also supports a more expansive surround-sound setup, allowing you to pair up to four compatible HomePod speakers instead of just two.
Three more Verge-approved deals:
- If you’ve been meaning to pick up Pikmin 4, Walmart is selling a digital copy for $39.88 ($20 off), which is a great price considering most other retailers are still charging the full $59.99. It’s the original Switch version, but you can upgrade to the forthcoming Nintendo Switch 2 Edition when it arrives on November 12th by purchasing a separate $9.99 upgrade pack, which adds improved graphics and a new Dandori Academy mode. That brings your total to just $49.87, saving you about $20 compared to buying the $69.99 Switch 2 Edition outright. Read our review.
- All eyes might be on the iPhone Duo — which is now available to preorder, despite shipments being delayed into 2027 — but if you have a non-foldable iPhone, Woot is currently discounting a wide range of Otterbox cases through October 31st. I’ve owned several of the brand’s cases for both my smartphones and tablets over the years, and I’ve been impressed by their durability. I currently use the OtterBox Symmetry Series Clear Case for my iPhone 16, which normally costs $49.99 but is now available in various colors for just $5.99 with a 90-day warranty. The sale also includes cases for other iPhones, as well as some Samsung and Google phones, so it’s worth browsing even if you’re not planning to upgrade your phone anytime soon.
- Fanttik’s S1 Pro electric screwdriver is on sale for $45.99 ($44 off) at Amazon, which is $5 shy of its best price to date. It’s a handy cordless option for small tasks ranging from tightening screws to assembling desks, with 16 S2 hardened steel bits for tackling a variety of jobs. The USB-C rechargeable screwdriver also comes with a 220RPM motor and three torque settings, along with a LED light to help illuminate your workspace.

articles.title: MapQuest now shows Flock and other surveillance cameras on its map
articles.text:
MapQuest has added a surveillance layer to its app that shows known outdoor cameras and licence plate readers, including those made by Flock Safety. Users can switch it on in Map Options, next to the traffic and incidents layers. The update follows a surge in MapQuest downloads in September.
MapQuest has added a layer to its app that shows where known outdoor surveillance cameras and licence plate readers are, Engadget reported on Friday. Users can turn it on in Map Options, where it sits next to the traffic and incidents layers.
The layer includes cameras from Flock Safety, one of the largest makers of licence plate readers in the US. It also shows devices from Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, and Verkada.
MapQuest announced the feature on social media with the line “The Roads Have Eyes!”, according to CarScoops. The site added that the camera locations are crowdsourced, so users can add devices they spot.
Licence plate readers photograph passing cars and log their plates, times, and locations. Police and private groups can then search those records.
Flock’s cameras have been spreading fast across the US, and they face growing pushback. A US judge has also ruled that a police Flock search was unconstitutional mass surveillance.
The update is the latest in a run of changes at MapQuest. Downloads of the app jumped in September after it refused to follow Google Maps and Apple Maps in relabelling Lake Ontario as Lake America.
It has since added Android Auto support and public transport directions, according to Engadget.

articles.title: VCCI kiến nghị sửa quy định giá xăng dầu, ‘áp đặt giá bán bất hợp lý’
articles.text:
Liên đoàn Thương mại và Công nghiệp Việt Nam (VCCI) vừa góp ý về Dự thảo Nghị định về kinh doanh xăng dầu của Bộ Công Thương.
Trong đó, về cơ chế giá, kê khai giá và giám sát cạnh tranh, VCCI cho rằng việc trao quyền quyết định giá cho doanh nghiệp phù hợp với khoản 1 Điều 8 Luật Giá số 16/2023/QH15.
Tuy nhiên, khi lợi nhuận do thương nhân tự xác định, công thức giá tại Điều 28 cần được sử dụng làm căn cứ để minh bạch hóa, giải trình và giám sát quá trình hình thành giá, thay vì trở thành công cụ áp đặt mức lợi nhuận hoặc chi phí ngoài phạm vi pháp luật quy định.
Bên cạnh đó, yêu cầu phân tích biến động từng yếu tố so với lần điều chỉnh liền trước trong mỗi lần điều chỉnh giá có thể tạo gánh nặng lớn cho doanh nghiệp nhỏ, nhất là khi giá được điều chỉnh thường xuyên.
Vì vậy, việc kiểm tra cần tập trung vào tính chính xác, trung thực của dữ liệu và việc tuân thủ các quy định về giá, cạnh tranh, đồng thời bảo đảm quyền tự quyết định giá của thương nhân.
Chỉ ra sự trùng lặp giữa điểm b và điểm c khoản 2 Điều 28 về giá bán của thương nhân phân phối độc lập, VCCI cho rằng cơ quan soạn thảo cần hợp nhất các nội dung này hoặc phân định rõ phạm vi áp dụng.
Đối với quy định về giá bán của thương nhân phân phối độc lập tại địa bàn xa, VCCI đề nghị làm rõ căn cứ pháp lý và khả năng phản ánh chi phí thực tế của doanh nghiệp.
Cụ thể, theo khoản 2 Điều 27, thương nhân đầu mối được quyết định giá bán tại địa bàn xa trên cơ sở chi phí thực tế. Trong khi đó, thương nhân phân phối độc lập bị giới hạn bởi mức giá cao nhất do thương nhân đầu mối công bố tại cùng địa bàn, dù điều kiện vận chuyển và quy mô kinh doanh có thể khác nhau.
VCCI đề nghị cần xem xét lại sự khác biệt này, bảo đảm cơ chế giá phản ánh phù hợp điều kiện kinh doanh thực tế. Đồng thời, đối với quy định cho phép áp dụng giá tối đa, khung giá hoặc giá cụ thể khi phát hiện dấu hiệu giá tăng bất hợp lý, dự thảo cần làm rõ điều kiện, thẩm quyền và trình tự thực hiện.
Trường hợp đây là biện pháp bình ổn giá, việc áp dụng phải tuân thủ pháp luật về giá và trình tự quy định tại Điều 31, tránh hình thành cơ chế can thiệp song song chỉ dựa trên những dấu hiệu chưa được xác định rõ.
Về giám sát cạnh tranh, theo VCCI, quy định tại khoản 3 Điều 29 cần được rà soát để bảo đảm phù hợp với Luật Cạnh tranh. Theo cơ quan này, việc đưa ngưỡng thị phần kết hợp 30% vào dự thảo có thể dẫn đến cách hiểu rằng phạm vi phát hiện, xử lý hành vi thỏa thuận hạn chế cạnh tranh bị thu hẹp.
VCCI nhấn mạnh, biến động khách quan của các yếu tố hình thành giá cần được xem xét khi đánh giá hành vi, nhưng không nên trở thành điều kiện loại trừ việc xem xét thỏa thuận hạn chế cạnh tranh.
VCCI cũng đề nghị làm rõ khái niệm “áp đặt giá bán bất hợp lý”, theo hướng dẫn chiếu đến hành vi tương ứng được quy định trong Luật Cạnh tranh.
VCCI đề xuất đơn giản hóa thủ tục kê khai giá
Đối với quy định về kê khai giá, VCCI cho biết thương nhân phân phối thuộc hệ thống đầu mối vẫn có quyền quyết định giá bán thấp hơn mức giá đầu mối công bố và không bắt buộc phải tăng giá khi đầu mối tăng giá theo điểm a khoản 2 Điều 28.
Tuy nhiên, nếu thương nhân áp dụng đúng mức giá đã được đầu mối kê khai, việc yêu cầu kê khai riêng sẽ tạo ra thủ tục trùng lặp. Ngoài ra, thời hạn kê khai chậm nhất vào cuối ngày làm việc tiếp theo kể từ ngày giá mới có hiệu lực tại điểm đ khoản 2 Điều 29 có thể tạo áp lực tuân thủ, nhất là với những doanh nghiệp chưa có khả năng kê khai tự động.
Vì vậy, VCCI đề nghị rà soát thời hạn này trong mối tương quan với quy định chung về kê khai giá tại Nghị định số 85/2024/NĐ-CP.
Từ những phân tích trên, VCCI kiến nghị sửa đổi các quy định theo hướng sử dụng công thức giá làm căn cứ kê khai, giải trình và giám sát quá trình hình thành giá, không dùng để áp đặt mức lợi nhuận hoặc chi phí ngoài phạm vi pháp luật.
Song song đó, cần đơn giản hóa hồ sơ tính giá đối với thương nhân phân phối nhưng vẫn bảo đảm khả năng kiểm tra tính chính xác, trung thực của dữ liệu; hợp nhất hoặc phân định rõ phạm vi áp dụng.
Về giá bán tại địa bàn xa, VCCI đề xuất chỉ áp dụng giá tối đa trong thời gian bình ổn giá hoặc cho phép thương nhân phân phối áp dụng cơ chế phản ánh chi phí thực tế tương tự quy định tại khoản 2 Điều 27. Việc áp dụng giá tối đa, khung giá hoặc giá cụ thể với tư cách biện pháp bình ổn giá phải thực hiện theo trình tự tại Điều 31.
Đối với giám sát cạnh tranh, VCCI kiến nghị sửa khoản 3 Điều 29 theo hướng giao Bộ Công Thương và UBND cấp tỉnh theo dõi dữ liệu kê khai giá, phát hiện dấu hiệu vi phạm và chuyển thông tin, tài liệu đến cơ quan có thẩm quyền xem xét, đồng thời bỏ ngưỡng thị phần kết hợp 30%.
Liên quan đến việc kê khai giá, VCCI đề xuất cho phép kê khai một lần thông qua hệ thống kết nối dữ liệu, không yêu cầu kê khai riêng đối với thương nhân phân phối áp dụng đúng mức giá đã được đầu mối kê khai.
Nếu quyết định mức giá khác, thương nhân thực hiện kê khai bằng phương thức điện tử đơn giản. Thời hạn kê khai chậm nhất vào cuối ngày làm việc tiếp theo chỉ nên áp dụng khi việc kê khai được thực hiện tự động; các trường hợp còn lại cần thống nhất với quy định chung về kê khai giá.

articles.title: ‘More countries coming very soon’: Ramp after its $60bn valuation
articles.text:
“Today, Ramp raised $1.85B at a $60B valuation,” Eric Oancea, who leads Ramp in Europe, wrote on LinkedIn.
His post confirms the round that Bloomberg reported on 10 October. Ramp’s co-founders, Eric Glyman and Karim Atiyeh, marked the new valuation with a blog post on 15 October, titled “Ramp at $60B: The End of the Beginning”.
The post gives new figures. According to Ramp, 85,000 businesses use it, and it saves them more than $1bn a month. It passed $2bn in annualised revenue over the summer, with positive cash flow.
In September alone, Ramp says, it saved customers 1.5 million hours. The founders compare that to giving 9,000 people a working month back.
Two raises in six months
Oancea wrote that he joined Ramp less than six months ago, and that this is already his second raise there. He listed what changed in that time.
The valuation went from $32bn to $60bn, and annualised revenue from over $1bn to over $2bn. Customers rose from 65,000 to 85,000. The average saving for customers grew from 5% to 7.5% of their spend. Ramp went from no markets outside the US to three.
In June, Ramp raised $750m at a $44bn valuation. Neither Ramp’s post nor Oancea’s names the investors in the new round.
Europe is next
Ramp went live in the UK on 15 September with corporate cards, expense management, bill payments and accounting automation, according to its launch post. In March it bought Billhop, a fintech based in Stockholm.
Ramp now adds more than 100 UK customers a month, Oancea wrote. He offered to onboard new customers himself, adding that they do not need to wait for their current contracts to run out.
“Job’s not finished. We are just getting started. More countries coming very soon,” Oancea wrote, with an EU flag.
What Ramp built this year
The founders listed the products Ramp launched this year. They include Stack, for closing the books faster, Accounts Receivable, AI Spend Management and Router, which picks the right AI model. There is also Glass, so a team only has to learn things once.
“Plus 476 more features. It’s only October,” they wrote.
“Chapter 1 was about what we could build. Chapter 2 is about what you can,” Glyman and Atiyeh wrote.

articles.title: Analogue is re-releasing its SNES and Genesis consoles with some nice upgrades
articles.text:
Analogue announced new versions of its Super Nt and Mega Sg retro consoles today with a “reworked industrial design” and built-in wireless connectivity for controllers and accessories. Like the original versions, the new Super Nt Plus and Mega Sg Plus are able to play Nintendo and Sega Genesis cartridges using an FPGA processor that perfectly recreates the functionality of Nintendo and Sega’s 16-bit consoles without the need for emulation.
Analogue is re-releasing its SNES and Genesis consoles with some nice upgrades
The Super Nt Plus and Mega Sg Plus add USB-C and USB-A ports plus built-in wireless connections for controllers.
Although neither of the new consoles allows SNES or Genesis titles to be played in 4K like the Analogue 3D does with Nintendo 64 titles, the 1080p Super Nt and Mega Sg Plus add a USB-C port so you can power them with the cables you already use with your phone and mobile devices, and an additional USB-A port for other peripherals. Both consoles also introduce a built-in Bluetooth or a low-latency 2.4Ghz wireless connection for connecting to gamepads without requiring an additional controller port dongle.
Wired controllers are still an option, and the upgraded consoles can both be powered up remotely using whatever gamepad is connected as the primary controller. Analogue also says game cartridges can now be hot swapped without having to completely power down either console after quitting the game through a menu.
Both the Super Nt Plus and Mega Sg Plus will be available for preorder starting on October 19th at 9AM PT/11AM ET for $219.99 with shipping expected to start sometime in December, later this year.

articles.title: Accenture caps staff Claude spending at $29 a month
articles.text:
“Providing a WBS and obtaining a license does not guarantee indefinite or ongoing access to Claude.”
Accenture gave its staff that warning in an internal announcement about Claude, Anthropic’s AI model. The consulting firm now pays only $29 a month per person for Claude use, Joseph Cox reported for 404 Media on 15 October.
Some Accenture employees had been spending as much as $1,000 a month. The change took effect on 1 October, according to the announcement, which 404 Media has seen.
Accenture titled it “Claude Enterprise Users: Important Updates to Licensing and Usage Costs”.
Who pays for the rest
The announcement says that “all costs are consumption-based”. Above the $29, an employee has to charge the extra use to a Work Breakdown Structure, or WBS. That is Accenture’s budget code for a specific project or team.
Premium plans come with $250 of token usage a week, 404 Media reported. Many employees are on the General plan instead.
The announcement also says Claude Enterprise stays available based on role and business need. Accenture reviews licences periodically and may move them to where they bring the most value.
Employees try to upgrade
Some employees now want Premium accounts, so that their projects avoid paying for the extra use. That is according to internal messages 404 Media viewed. One employee said their usage costs were above $500, as they had been in past months.
“How can I speed up the upgrade to a premium account? This obviously has a significant impact on project costs,” the employee wrote.
Another said they use Claude Code “extensively” to build and test an AI accelerator for several Accenture clients. Their usage usually runs between $500 and $1,000 a month. A third employee said Accenture had revoked their Claude access altogether.
What Accenture says
An Accenture spokesperson told 404 Media that the company makes AI available to all its people.
“Our approach today is to provide the right tool for the right work, and we continue to invest in AI capabilities, skills and enablement that deliver greater value for clients and our own organization,” the spokesperson said.
Accenture has about 799,000 people and serves about 9,000 clients, according to its own figures. In September it invested in Within, an AI platform company, to help clients deploy AI agents.
The announcement cited Accenture’s own survey, in which 82% of more than 3,000 executives said they are increasing AI investment. 404 Media saw a “special irony” here. Accenture has encouraged clients to invest heavily in AI, and is now curbing its own staff’s use.
Other companies have already moved to cap employee AI spending. Microsoft set AI budgets for its divisions in August, and Atlassian’s engineers now work to an AI budget too. Uber’s technology chief said the tokenmaxxing era is ending.

articles.title: A fake WhatsApp clone is showing up before the real version on the Play Store
articles.text:
After a Chrome clone was spotted on the Play Store earlier this week, a user on Reddit says they’re seeing a fake version of WhatsApp in a “sponsored” slot above the real version. As reported earlier by Android Authority, the WhatsApp dupe has racked up over 500,000 downloads and, at the time of writing, its Play Store listing is still live.
A fake WhatsApp clone is showing up before the real version on the Play Store
The ‘WhatsApp Messenger’ dupe reportedly popped up as a sponsored result above the real version.
Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The WhatsApp clone is from a developer going by “Agment Assets sallu” who doesn’t currently have anything else listed on the Play Store. Their listing for the WhatsApp impostor has the same icon, screenshots, and text as the real version, but the real WhatsApp has over 10 billion downloads, an “editor’s choice” badge, and over 246 million reviews. Android Authority points out that the WhatsApp clone may be using Google Play’s Early Access program to disable public user reviews, which could have helped users warn people against downloading the app.

articles.title: Epic says it vibe coded its new launcher because ‘programming is hard’
articles.text:
“Programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher.”
Epic Games opened its launcher announcement with those lines on 14 October. Epic says the rebuilt app is faster than the old one and has a new look. It is out in Preview for Windows, macOS and, for the first time, Linux.
Vibe coding usually means building software mostly through prompts to AI models, with little code written by hand.
The announcement came two days after Jason Schreier reported for Bloomberg that Epic had delayed its Disney game. Epic also told that team to go “AI first”, Bloomberg reported. Chief executive Tim Sweeney then said the company was in the middle of a “huge pivot” towards AI.
‘No more hand-written code’
The game is an unannounced shooter with Marvel and Star Wars characters. Disney invested $1.5bn in Epic in 2024, and the two agreed a multi-game partnership that was set to start with this shooter. It had been due in March 2027. Epic has now pushed it back without a new date, according to people familiar with the project.
Epic told the developers to use tools such as Anthropic’s Claude, with humans managing and guiding the work. “No more hand-written code,” one of the game’s directors told staff in an internal message that Bloomberg reviewed. The director added that all art for the game would be “generated with full AI workflows”.
Some developers were stunned when Epic announced the change on a video call, the people told Bloomberg. Some joked about whether they should ask Claude to fix its own mistakes. Others argued it would not work as well as Epic hoped. Progress on the game had already been slower than expected, the people said, because Epic underestimated the staff and time it needed.
‘A huge pivot’
Jake Jones, Epic’s communications director, gave Bloomberg a statement. Disney did not immediately respond to Bloomberg.
“We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do,” Jones said.
Sweeney posted on X shortly after the report.
“We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration. The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people,” Sweeney wrote.
He added that the goal is to let everyone at Epic build “MORE and BETTER stuff”.
In March, Epic laid off more than 1,000 employees. Sweeney blamed a fall in Fortnite engagement. In a note to staff, he wrote that “the layoffs aren’t related to AI”. Epic is also building Claude and Gemini into Unreal Engine 6.
A launcher built ‘from scratch’
Martin Keely, general manager of the Epic Games Store, told PC Gamer the team used AI to write new code. It did not reuse the old app’s code.
“We started from scratch. This is a completely new architecture for both the store and the launcher shell,” Keely said.
Epic says the new launcher starts in 5.47 seconds, against 10.07 seconds for Steam. Keywords Studios ran those tests for Epic in October. It averaged results across 13 machines, leaving out the three lowest-end machines it tested. Ars Technica found in its own tests that the launcher reaches the store a few seconds faster than Steam.
Epic calls this first release “a speedboat and not a yacht”. The Preview still lacks some social features and account options from the old launcher. It does not support Intel Macs.
Not everyone liked the pitch. On Bluesky, Chris Franklin called the opening line “absolutely jawdropping” from a company “once renowned for their engine prowess”. Sweeney joked on X, in a reply to a Fortnite on Linux account: “we vibecoded linux support”.
Fortnite is coming to Linux
The bigger news for Linux players is Fortnite. Epic is rebuilding its Easy Anti-Cheat software as EAC Linux v2, and will test it in Fortnite first.
The new version does not use a kernel driver. It checks for a signed kernel, Secure Boot, TPM 2.0, measured boot and other security features already in Linux. It only runs while a protected game is open. Epic says it is talking to distribution maintainers, and to Valve about Steam Hardware devices. The Steam Deck does not support the required features yet.
Epic has given no date. Engineering director Rick Deist told The Verge there is no timeline for the Linux version of Fortnite.

articles.title: A week with RTX Spark: everything we’ve learned using Nvidia’s new laptops
articles.text:
Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X processor is finally here, and we’ve been collectively testing a small fortune’s worth of powerful laptops sporting this new “superchip.” RTX Spark is designed to be a high-performing Arm-based SoC for laptops and small desktop computers, rivaling the best from Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. It has loads of cores, Nvidia RTX Blackwell graphics, and enough power and unified memory to run sizable local AI models.
A week with RTX Spark: everything we’ve learned using Nvidia’s new laptops
Nvidia’s new Arm-based laptop chip is an exciting new challenger, but exclusively for the high-end.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
The flagship placement is inside Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra with a staggering 128GB of unified memory, which our own Tom Warren fully reviewed. Sean Hollister has been testing a 64GB version of the Asus ProArt P16, which I’ve also been testing in its top-spec 128GB config. Since I’m the most spoiled of the lot, I also have a 64GB Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 and a 32GB HP OmniBook Ultra in for testing.
All of these laptops have the same N1X chip with 20 CPU cores and 6,144 GPU CUDA cores, and they’re all wildly expensive — ranging from the HP OmniBook at $3,199.99 to the Asus ProArt’s $6,999.99. There’s an 18-core / 5,120 CUDA N1X chip in lower cost configs, but that only gets as cheap as $2,599.99 for a Surface Laptop Ultra or a smaller Asus ProArt P14 with 24GB of RAM.
These are big and expensive laptops built on new chips. They’re meant for developers, coders, and content creators who might also want the ability to use local AI and even play games using the latest Nvidia tech like DLSS 5. There’s a lot to test, and we have not had a ton of time to test it all. So below you won’t find an exhaustive scored review of any one laptop, but instead our impressions and thoughts from three writers using five laptops for a week.
Is Nvidia’s “superchip” really all that super? Are Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm officially on notice? Have any of us gotten any sleep?
Does it just work?
Antonio Di Benedetto: Windows on Arm is no longer a wholly subpar experience like it was a few years ago. Thanks in large part to the push around Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, lots of development has been put into native Arm-based apps for Windows. And many x86 apps work fine via Microsoft’s Prism emulation layer.
Adobe has had native Arm versions of Photoshop and Premiere for some time now, and even though my precious Lightroom Classic is still an x86-based app I don’t notice any issues using it on Arm. At this point, you’ve gotta be relying on specialized software that’s exclusively x86 based for Windows on Arm to be a non-starter — or you want to freely play any games out there without any worry of incompatibilities.
Sean Hollister: Every so often, there’s that moment when an app takes longer to load than it should, and I wonder whether it’ll load at all. Even then, it typically loads. Occasionally, it takes more than one try. My Evernote notes disappeared a few times one day when I alt-tabbed away, but a force refresh fixed that. And apps don’t seem to respect my system preference for dark mode.
But I largely agree with Antonio. I made an RTX Spark my daily driver, with all my typical work and personal apps — Signal, Discord, Audacity, CapCut and Evernote, Irfanview, Slack, ScreenToGif and more — and nothing has failed me so far. I never once needed to think whether I was running an Arm or an x86 app. The real hitches came with gaming and AI, as you’ll read below.
Tom Warren: I’ve been using a Windows on Arm laptop with a Qualcomm chip daily for the past two years and things have improved to the point that I can’t tell if an app is native or not anymore. That’s the same story on the RTX Spark laptops, and I feel like Nvidia’s entry into this category will only improve the story for creative apps and gaming.
Can it game?
TW: Windows on Arm never looked like a serious gaming platform before now. While there still aren’t many native Arm games, Nvidia’s GPU helps bruteforce through the emulation layer. Your mileage in gaming is going to vary depending on the title, but for the most part I’ve found that medium settings, running at 1440p and DLSS performance, will get you to a stable 60fps in most games.
I mostly game on my desktop, where I’m spoiled by using an RTX 5090 on a 32-inch 4K screen every day with maxed-out game settings, but I didn’t mind the look of medium settings on a 15-inch display. I was able to run Black Myth: Wukong at 70fps on average at native resolution (3270 x 2180) with medium settings and DLSS performance mode enabled. I ran the same medium settings and DLSS performance in Cyberpunk 2077 and averaged 66fps, and Forza Horizon 6 managed an average of 57fps.
In some titles you may need to drop the resolution or settings lower, though. This definitely isn’t as good as a dedicated gaming laptop, but for something that’s roughly on the level of a MacBook Pro it’s more than good enough for gaming on the go.
SH: Like Tom says, the GPU power is there — but the CPU might hold back some of your games. I had plenty of power for a smooth 60fps in Returnal (at 1440p with high settings), Expedition 33 (at a DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with high settings), Jedi Survivor (DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with medium settings), and Shadow of the Tomb Raider (at native 1800p and highest spec).
But when I fired up Helldivers 2, even dipping down to a DLSS-upscaled 1080p was no guarantee of 60fps in the highest difficulty missions. There are just too many enemies on screen for the Spark to keep up. Star Wars Zero Company is even more CPU-bound — the Spark didn’t care whether I was maximizing or minimizing the graphics and screen resolution. No matter what I tried, I typically saw my framerate capped between 37fps and 39fps in battle.
Even ancient and low-powered games can have quirks. I tried the 2003 title Max Payne 2 and saw situations where framerate dipped to 50fps. I even saw a few hitches in the excellent UFO 50, a collection of 2D games, though a couple other 2D games ran great.
I’m also not sure if RTX Spark is suitable for VR yet. The excellent Titanfall 2 VR mod worked, and it seemed to run fine at first, but lost a little stability after a few minutes. That could be my Wi-Fi, because the driver for Valve’s Steam Frame wireless adapter wouldn’t install on the Spark. Neither did Steam’s streaming audio solution, so the audio came out of the Nvidia laptop instead of the headset.
Just so we’re clear, all of this is assuming you want a laptop maxing out its fans and positively dumping heat on your desk or lap. That’s not unusual for thin gaming notebooks, but it’s way louder and hotter than a good desktop or handheld.
|  | 2560x1600 | 2560x1600 | 2560x1600 | 2560x1600 | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
|  | Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark (20-core, 6144 CUDA, 128GB RAM) | HP OmniBook Ultra RTX Spark (20-core, 6144 CUDA, 32GB RAM) | Framework Laptop 16 5070 (2025, 8GB VRAM) | MacBook Pro M5 Max | 
| Black Myth: Wukong TSR | 27 | 27 | 28 | Not compatible | 
| Black Myth: Wukong DLSS | 41 | 44 | 45 | Not compatible | 
| Black Myth: Wukong DLSS FG | 53 | 59 | 71 | Not compatible | 
| Cyberpunk 2077 Ultra | 41 | 46 | 57 | 56 | 
| Cyberpunk 2077 Ultra RT & DLSS quality | 30 | 35 | 44 | 42 (MetalFX Quality) | 
| Cyberpunk 2077 Ultra RT & DLSS Frame Gen x2 | 53 | 56 | 68 | 75 (MetalFX Quality, FSR 3.1 FG) | 
| Cyberpunk 2077 Ultra RT & DLSS Frame Gen x4 | 92 | 103 | Not tested | Not compatible | 
AD: I’ve wanted a MacBook Pro-like laptop with full PC gaming chops for as long as I can remember, so I was hyped for these laptops to deliver the goods in graphics. The first night, I set up the Asus ProArt P16, with all 128GB of its ridiculously large pool of memory, and when I booted up Big Walk for my planned online evening with some friends my first thought was, “Well, that looks okay. I guess.” I know Big Walk isn’t some triple-A graphical titan, but it has some fairly demanding graphics for the “friend slop” genre. I expected the N1X to max it out, or at least get close, but not really.
I had to bump the P16’s 4K display down to 2560 x 1600, and instead of Big Walk’s Highest or Very high graphics presets, I brought it down to High to maintain a decently solid 60-ish fps. Does any of that really matter for this silly co-op game about solving puzzles with your buddies? Of course not. It looked fine, after all. But it was a sobering reminder that this “superchip” is no graphical magician.
As Tom and Sean point out, RTX Spark can do some decent gaming, but temper your expectations for medium or even low settings in some cases, and be ready to rely on DLSS and frame gen. There’s no denying that cheaper desktops and even laptops with discrete Nvidia graphics cards can easily beat out an N1X. Nvidia claims it’s like having an RTX 5070 Laptop GPU in an SoC, but in my testing it was somewhere between that and an RTX 5060 Laptop GPU — not a slouch, for sure, but if you’re a gamer first your money goes much further with traditional Nvidia graphics cards.
How’s the battery life?
SH: Nvidia’s partners saw fit to equip their first wave of RTX Spark laptops with some of the biggest batteries you can bring on an airplane with no questions asked — but even with a 99.9 watt-hour pack like the one in my Asus ProArt P16, these laptops won’t be winning awards for longevity. While Tom and Antonio spent their days testing every use case under the sun, I made the P16 my daily driver for normal work while watching the battery meter like a hawk. That mostly means writing stories in a web browser, and it’s not quite lasting the day.
My best run was 5 hours and 40 minutes of real-world work at 50 percent brightness, including an hour-long video call with Tom and Antonio to strategize our RTX Spark coverage plan. The next day, I got only about 5 hours from a full charge because I spent two of them editing this video in Capcut. The third time I drained the battery, it took 5 hours, too.
With web work, I’m typically seeing 13-17 watt battery drain on the laptop’s default settings, but that climbs to 20-30 watts with light video work, up to 50 watts during the (brief) Capcut video export, and I made it jump all the way to 120 watts playing Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. The battery couldn’t keep feeding at that rate — it slowly went down, and at 30 percent charge I saw a big performance hit as it dropped dramatically to 60 watts.
The good news is the Asus charges fast from a 140W USB-C PD power source. It took 20 minutes to go from dead to 50 percent battery, another 15 minutes to get to 70 percent, and a total of 1 hour, 15 minutes to reach 95 percent charge.
AD: I’ve had to run lots of benchmarks while plugged in, so I haven’t been able to spend as much time testing battery life as I’d normally like. Anecdotally, in lots of fits and starts, battery life seems solid. As Sean saw, you’re unlikely to get through a full eight hour work day unless you’re going out of your way to be efficient. And if you fire up anything heavy, like a local AI model (more on that in a minute), you won’t even make it to lunch. I’ll eventually do more thorough battery testing as I continue using these laptops, including our usual rundown tests for a bit of 1:1 comparisons.
Does local AI seem useful?
TW: Not yet. It all feels like a beta aimed at developers right now: from the install experience of AI agents flashing up command prompts and Visual Studio, to the fans blasting away for the most basic of queries.
I struggled to come up with many compelling use cases for the power of these chips for local AI work. A lot of tasks could simply be done far more quickly and without the laptop fans spinning up by using a free cloud model. The power here is really in leaving the agent running at full throttle to build something overnight, running tasks that developers would favor.
It’s also nice to have this all on a local device, without having to share emails and files with a cloud service and worry about the privacy aspects. Still, I would regularly close OpenClaw or Hermes and not let them run in the background all day, especially if I had given them permissions to access local files. I’m just not ready to trust AI fully, local or not.
Microsoft and Nvidia both envision a future where AI agents automate things on your PC, but I’m still not fully convinced. While there are some mundane tasks I could certainly automate, I like using my PC to edit photos or videos, write, and play games. I don’t want to sit there and watch a robot do all of that for me. That’s part of the joy of computing to me.
SH: I walked out of Nvidia’s Editor’s Day thinking I might finally have a reason to fire up local AI. I asked Hermes, running Qwen3.8-27B, to build me a daily news briefing much like the one in Nvidia’s on-stage demo. It took 10 minutes, and 10 percent of my entire 99.9 watt-hour battery, to finally produce a list of stories that took the cloud-based Claude (Opus 5.5) half as long — while utterly monopolizing my GPU and dramatically heating up the Spark laptop. The laptop stayed hot and a little sluggish as long as I kept Hermes open.
Claude also produced better results, with more detail and better sourcing. I guess I got the local AI tokens for “free,” I wouldn’t trust Claude with my email, and I probably could have used a smaller, lighter model. But I went with what the program recommended, and that was the result. I tried a clean reinstall of Hermes to make sure it wasn’t a misconfiguration, but this time, the prompt took even longer and used 60 percent of my battery. Ouch.
AD: I’m still early in my journey of learning to use local AI, and these RTX Spark laptops are obviously a viable — albeit, expensive — option. But even if you have 128GB of memory to use some chunky models, it’s still not a user-friendly experience for beginners. Microsoft’s Get Started intro in Windows 11 gives you easy one-click installs for Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, and Perplexity. (Which all have ESRB ratings for some reason?) But after that, you’re kind of on your own. I stuck with Hermes, since that’s what I was already using on the Mac Studio, but if you’re using it on a system with 32GB of RAM or less it just tells you there isn’t enough memory for its recommended local Qwen models — either routing you towards the cloud or fully relying on you to go fetch a smaller model on your own.
Using local AI has major privacy advantages over cloud models, but it’s definitely less convenient since local LLMs are much slower to process and more taxing on your system. Churning a local model through your laptop’s memory tears through any of these laptops’ large batteries, and the results from LLMs are still mixed. I burned through 30 percent of the Lenovo Yoga 9n’s battery in 36 minutes to get a Qwen 3.8 27B model to resize and add a white background to five product images in PNG format — and it cropped the images wrong and cut off the products. I got it to do it right after a couple follow-up prompts, and grabbing the power cable to prevent Hermes from killing the laptop in the process.
Is the hardware truly great?
AD: These laptops are very expensive, but that also means the manufacturers are mostly bringing their A-games. Across the Asus, HP, Lenovo, and what I gathered from Tom’s thoughts on the Surface, the RTX Spark line is awash in great-to-excellent haptic trackpads, keyboards, screens, and speakers. The metal builds of the three I’m testing feel great to the touch. The OLED displays all look fantastic. And each of these are decently thin for the kind of workstation-class laptops that they are.
If I had to pick one for myself based on hardware alone I’d probably choose the Asus ProArt. It ticks the most boxes for me with its three USB-C ports, super bright display, superior inverted-T arrow cluster, and full SD card slot. The HP actually feels the nicest, with an impressively rock-solid chassis, but at nearly five pounds it’s the heaviest of the bunch, and its microSD card slot is much less useful to me.
As for the Lenovo, it’s actually been my sleeper favorite. It’s the only 2-in-1 in this crop I’ve been testing, and that just makes it more flexible (pun intended) and fun. You can use its large stylus on either the screen or the large trackpad, giving it lots more potential for graphics and design work. And tent mode with a large 16-inch 120Hz OLED is a delight for the occasional gaming session or watching shows and movies — it’s just not as bright as the Asus.
SH: I’ve only truly driven the Asus P16 so far, but I was impressed with the build quality of the whole spectrum of RTX Spark launch laptops at Nvidia’s Editor’s Day. The Asus P16 probably wouldn’t be my pick personally because of its extra glossy screen and oversensitive touchpad. I like to use my laptops in rooms with lots of ambient light, and find I have to crank up the brightness of this machine’s otherwise excellent calibrated OLED screen. Meanwhile, my palms keep tapping my mouse cursor on things I didn’t mean to tap, just because they accidentally brush the touchpad while typing.
The speakers and webcam also leave something to be desired, but the Windows Hello face login and proximity sensing are excellent. As soon as I walk away, the screen dims, and I’m logged right back in just by looking at my laptop. Despite the heat, Asus’ fans aren’t shrill — they’re very loud and noticeable while gaming, but at least it’s whoosh rather than whine.
TW: While I ran into some weird bugs with the Surface Laptop Ultra during testing, I can’t fault the hardware. The look and feel is very similar to a MacBook Pro, and the magnetic USB-C port really feels like something Apple should have done — it’s that good. The large haptic trackpad carries on the tradition of great Surface trackpads, with the added benefit of subtle haptic feedback when you move windows around or align objects in apps like PowerPoint.
I would have preferred an OLED display on the Laptop Ultra, but I found switching away from the default “Vivid” color option to “Enhanced” improved the contrast on the mini-LED panel. I also really appreciate the port section on the Laptop Ultra, especially that there’s a full SD card reader and even a USB-A port. Check out my full review for more thoughts.
Is it fast? Does it hang with Apple M-series chips?
