AD: Yes, the RTX Spark N1X is a powerful chip. These high-end laptop configurations we’ve been testing with lots of unified memory are meant to compete with the Pro and Max chips in Apple’s MacBook Pros. And while they can hang in some GPU performance tests, like tying the top spec M5 Max in a Blender render, Apple’s CPUs are much more powerful.
Apple has put lots of development into its in-house processors and the extra-fast “super cores” of its M6, M5 Pro, and M5 Max chips. And, frankly, nothing competes with those chips in single core performance — not even Nvidia’s “superchip.” (Seriously, can we stop with the word super?) But the part that stings most about the RTX Spark’s 20-core CPU is that even a lowly 12-core M6 Mac Mini competes with it in multicore performance — and a Mac Mini starts at just $900.
It’s awesome to see this kind of graphics performance without the need for a discrete GPU, allowing for thinner system designs with less noisy fans. I’m into it, just as I was with AMD’s Strix Halo APU — but like Strix Halo, Nvidia’s RTX Spark is a pricey part. And there’s no denying that Apple’s offerings are more well-rounded performers, so long as you don’t care as much about games.
TW: It’s definitely up there, but I think Qualcomm comes closer to Apple’s M-series chips on the CPU side. Qualcomm also had years of experimentation with Windows on Arm before it acquired Nuvia and managed to create a competitive chip with the Snapdragon X series.
I think Nvidia will need a similar amount of work to catch up on the CPU side for future RTX Spark chips. The development of the RTX Spark took at least three years, and I had heard from sources familiar with Nvidia’s plans that the chips were supposed to launch last year. So work has been ongoing, but the CPU side is still a little disappointing.
Nvidia picked MediaTek for its Arm-based CPU, a chipmaker that is better known for the Wi-Fi hardware in laptops, not the CPUs. I sure hope the next-generation is more powerful. The whole time I’ve been testing the Surface Laptop Ultra I couldn’t help but think the forbidden dream would be a combination of a Qualcomm CPU and Nvidia GPU. I can’t see that ever happening in reality, but it would certainly be interesting to see.
So what’s our take on RTX Spark so far?
TW: I think it will elevate interest in Windows on Arm for creative and gaming tasks, simply because we haven’t had Arm-based Windows laptops that are really capable of running games until now. Nvidia is targeting creators and developers with its first round of RTX Spark laptops, but there’s definitely a gap here for a more affordable version focused on gaming. Perhaps that’s the N1 chips we’ve heard rumors about.
SH: Nice, but too pricey. Too hot and loud when you’re doing the things that would theoretically justify that price. I care what they stand for, and the direction they’re pointed, far more than I care to own one.
AD: I love that there is now even more competition in the laptop space, but the super high prices makes RTX Spark laptops mostly unattainable. I want to see lower cost options come around, as well as an eventual second generation with higher CPU performance to hopefully close the gap further with Apple. I also hope this helps push development for Arm-based and Arm-compatible games forward. Maybe it could even one day mean easier porting of games to macOS. Wouldn’t that be a fun outcome?
As cool as it will be to keep testing these super high-end RTX Spark models, I’m most hyped to get my hands on a base Surface Laptop Ultra or Asus ProArt P14 with 24GB of RAM and see how they stack up to the entry-level 14-inch M5 MacBook Pro. That’s my personal sweet spot for Apple’s lineup — the people’s MacBook Pro. (Well, okay, less these days now that it starts at two-grand.)
It’s an exciting time in computing when it comes to chip choice, but it’s also an absolutely cursed time thanks to RAMageddon and sky high prices. I’m constantly wondering what laptops like these RTX Sparks or even Googlebooks might have cost if AI demands didn’t drive up the prices of RAM and storage. I have no idea who is going to spend up to $7,000 on these laptops when PC sales as a whole seem on a downward trend, but it’s cool they exist.

articles.title: 5 midterm money takeaways: Democrats have candidate cash. Republicans have Elon Musk
articles.text:
One of the last big campaign-finance snapshots before the Nov. 3 Election Day is now available, and both political parties found something to like. But campaign cash is flowing in very different ways — and, on balance, points to an environment more favorable for Democrats.
On one side, Democratic candidates have turned into absolute cash cows, raising oodles more than their Republican rivals across Senate and House battlegrounds.
Republicans, however, still have a leg to stand on from an unprecedented flood of outside super PAC cash, bankrolled by a tiny circle of billionaires led by Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. The deluge of capital could be enough to stave off the worst of what has otherwise been a treacherous political environment for the GOP amid stubbornly high inflation and drooping approval ratings for President Donald Trump.
A flurry of Federal Election Commission filings Thursday at a key deadline detailed what candidates raised and spent from July through September and give insight into many of the outside groups backing them. More of the outside-money picture comes next week with another deadline for additional filings.
Here are CNBC's five takeaways:
Democratic grassroots strength
If Democrats want a financial case for a blue wave, start with the candidates themselves.
Democratic Senate nominees put up gaudy third-quarter totals. James Talarico raised $60.2 million in Texas, Jon Ossoff brought in $33.1 million in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed raised $30.7 million in Michigan. Sherrod Brown brought in $23.1 million in Ohio, while Troy Jackson raised $20.4 million in Maine, Mary Peltola $14.1 million in Alaska and Roy Cooper $12.2 million in North Carolina.
Even in reliably red Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton raised $9.4 million.
In several of those races, the Republican numbers were not even close. Ken Paxton raised about $10.2 million in Texas, Mike Rogers $9.7 million in Michigan, Susan Collins $5.2 million in Maine and Jon Husted $4.8 million in Ohio.
Candidate dollars are especially potent in the final stretch because campaigns control where they go and qualify for lower television advertising rates than super PACs do. In other words, Republicans may be able to make up a $1 fundraising gap with outside money — but it can cost them more than $1 to do it.
The same fundraising edge stretches into the House.
Democratic candidates outraised their Republican opponents through September in 13 of the 21 House races currently rated Toss Up by Cook, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. In North Carolina's 11th District, for example, Democrat Jamie Ager raised $2.1 million in the third quarter, compared with roughly $313,000 for Republican Jennifer Balkcom.
The fundraising surge coincides with a shifting map: the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter projected last week that Democrats could gain two to six Senate seats — enough to put the four-seat majority threshold within reach — and nine to 19 House seats, which would flip the chamber.
Republicans' ace in the hole
While Democratic candidates dominate direct donations, Republicans are countering with overwhelming outside spending.
The Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP's main Senate super PAC, raised a record $272.9 million from July through September, roughly $122 million more than its Democratic counterpart, according to FEC filings. On the House side, the Congressional Leadership Fund raised a record $94.4 million during the quarter and entered October with $156 million in cash, according to its FEC filing.
That outside money is functioning as a financial backstop for GOP candidates who trail badly in direct fundraising. Texas is the most extreme example: the SLF funneled $158 million into Texas PAC, the super PAC backing Paxton, according to FEC filings.
Elsewhere, Republicans have committed $15 million through the SLF to defend Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska, The Wall Street Journal reported this week. Outside groups account for roughly 80% of all ad buys in Alaska, where the SLF has spent $14 million backing Sen. Dan Sullivan, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data.
The blitz allowed Republicans to hold an aired-ad advantage in seven of eight top Senate battles and 25 of 42 contested House seats rated "Toss Up" or "Lean" Republican or Democrat by the Cook Report as of Oct. 9, according to AdImpact.
But polls have shown little movement in recent weeks, despite the advantage.
Musk fights for Texas
No donor better captures the scale — or the leverage — of that outside-money advantage than the world's richest person, Musk.
He pumped more than $276 million into federal political groups during the third quarter, making him the biggest known individual donor of the midterms. His disclosed giving included $158 million to Senate Leadership Fund and another $89 million to his America PAC, according to FEC filings.
Most of that capital was earmarked for a single rescue mission: Texas, the state that's his primary residence and headquarters of his businesses.
Musk gave the SLF $75 million on Sept. 9 and another $83 million on Sept. 23. Both times, the SLF transferred the exact same amount to Texas PAC the following day. The group, which is backing Paxton, reported no other donors through the end of September.
Until now, many national Republicans had been reluctant to sink resources into the Lone Star state's expensive media market while fighting across an already expanded Senate map. Musk effectively erased that trade-off, supplying enough money to build a dedicated financial firewall around Paxton without forcing the party to pull resources from other battlegrounds.
Democratic megadonors get off the sidelines
For months, Democrats worried over the reluctance of traditional megadonors to write checks following the 2024 election cycle with presidential contest drama at the top of the ticket. The latest filings suggest that freeze is thawing — though much money is still bypassing the Democratic National Committee.
Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and his wife, Cari Tuna, put about $16 million into the midterm fight this summer, according to FEC filings, while LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, who had also withheld money from the DNC this cycle, poured $11.5 million into the super PAC backing Talarico earlier this year.
The renewed megadonor money gives Democrats another source of firepower for the final weeks that can be quickly redirected if needed.
Already, Democrats' Senate Majority PAC raised a record $151 million in the third quarter and ended September with $112 million in cash, even as its Republican counterpart raised substantially more.
Record-breaking money
All the spending is feeding an election on track to shatter spending records.
AdImpact projects $11.6 billion in political advertising during the 2025-26 election cycle, which would make 2026 the most expensive cycle on record — surpassing both the $8.9 billion spent during the 2022 midterms and the $11.2 billion spent during the 2024 presidential cycle.
The congressional fight alone has already put $3.8 billion in advertising on the air, more than $870 million ahead of the comparable point in 2024, according to AdImpact. Senate races are helping drive the surge: the firm projects $3.4 billion in Senate advertising by the end of the cycle, up 48% from 2022.
But as the amount of money rises, some of it is becoming harder for voters to trace back to its original source.
Thursday's filings showed millions flowing into super PACs from nonprofits and other entities that are not required to disclose their own donors, leaving the original source of some of the cycle's biggest checks hidden.

articles.title: Why did CoreWeave stock get crushed this week? Look to this corner of the debt market for clues
articles.text: Mounting fears that CoreWeave's debt stress may signal a broader problem with the insatiable borrowing-driven artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out slammed tech stocks this week. The Nasdaq logged a weekly loss of 4.5%. CoreWeave stock plunged nearly 12% on Friday. Shares of the neocloud declined every day except Thursday, losing a quarter of their value since last Friday's close. Perhaps even more concerning than the stock rout has been the jump in CoreWeave corporate bond yields and spike in credit default swaps, a kind of insurance policy on debt. Corporate credit quality is getting a lot of attention these days, as funding costs increase due to above-target inflation that just won't quit and investor worries about the level of financial commitment being made by companies that don't want to be left behind in the AI race. We're obviously stock-focused investors around here, but in this wobbly moment for the AI trade, we cannot ignore what's happening in the corporate bond market. Credit default swaps help us get a more complete understanding. If they sound familiar, it may be because you've seen the movie "The Big Short," which focuses on the 2008 financial crisis. Hedge-fund manager Michael Burry, portrayed by Christian Bale, used credit default swaps as part of his bet against the U.S. housing industry. This week, the yield on a CoreWeave 2031 bond almost reached 16%. Friday, the yield stood around 14.5%. The instrument was issued in April at a 9.75% yield. At the same time, five-year CoreWeave CDS exceeded 1,000 basis points, up nearly 19% this week and 178% higher than they were 12 months ago. The CDS trading action puts the implied odds of a CoreWeave default within the next five years at around 60%, according to Bloomberg. The holder of debt can buy credit default swaps to protect against any losses resulting from issuer default. Like insurance, the amount paid is tied to the value and quality of the insured asset. To be sure, yields on a debt instrument are tied to the risk of default — when the risk goes up, so does the interest rate. Other factors also matter when it comes to the yield investors demand, such as inflation expectations, liquidity premiums, and the risk-free rate — usually measured by the 10-year Treasury yield , currently nearly 5.1%. A credit default swap, however, only reflects credit risk and none of those other aforementioned sentiment factors. As a result, a CDS can provide a more transparent picture of how investors actually feel about the debt issuer itself. For example, if an investor owns $1 million in debt issued by XYZ Corporation and wants to insure it, they could purchase a CDS. If the quote is 100 basis points, they would pay a premium of $10,000 (on an annual basis) to protect against default. An investor does not need to own the debt to buy a CDS — credit default swaps can also be bought and sold as ways to speculate on improvement or deterioration of a given company's credit quality. Apply that to CoreWeave CDS over at 1,000 basis points, and the cost to insure $1 million of CoreWeave debt goes above $100,000. So, why, as stock investors, do we care about insurance rates tied to the bond market? If we think of the things in our everyday lives that require insurance, it starts to make more sense. When you look to insure a home, or car, or anything for that matter, the premium you pay is based on two key factors: (1) the value of the item to be insured, which dictates the max payout in the event of a total loss; and (2) how risky it is to insure, factoring in the odds of the policy ever being triggered and the expected payout (as any residual value can offset the amount the insurer is ultimately on the hook for). It's that second point that we as stock investors care about. If the perceived risk of default increases, then that pushes up the quoted price for the CDS. The quoted price therefore acts as an easy-to-watch, real-time, quantifiable proxy for that risk. Obviously, the risk of default is something that should concern all stakeholders because equity value will generally be demolished long before any default actually happens. Those worries about debt risk are what's driving the CoreWeave situation. The stock is getting obliterated even though an actual default might never happen. And, according to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday, CoreWeave's financial position is stable and "improving every day." Huang's comments, which were made to Bloomberg at an event in Stockholm, were credited with reversing Thursday's earlier losses in CoreWeave and leading the stock to a higher close. Club name Nvidia is a big CoreWeave shareholder, and CoreWeave uses Nvidia chips to provide its clients with AI compute. Huang said Nvidia does not need to backstop CoreWeave because "their cost of capital is actually decreasing." Remember, risk and reward are tied at the hip. CDS rates, or more importantly, the move in the rate, can provide stock investors with a quick way to see what bond investors think. It's not an official credit quality rating, like those issued by S & P Global, Moody's, or Fitch. But what they lack in prominence, they make up for in pricing frequency, which can be far more useful to stock investors like us trying to better understand the market overall, as well as the price action of individual securities. Going back to the housing example, say you're considering a home on the beach but are concerned about the risk that a natural disaster can come in and damage or destroy the home. You could look to the listing price (think of this like the stock price) and try to figure out risk based on the pricing dynamics (is the house selling for more or less than it last sold, has it been sitting on the market a long time, have the sellers lowered the price to try and increase demand), or you can look into what has happened to the insurance rate on the property. The seller wants to get as much as they can. The insurer, on the other hand, is concerned with the risks posed to the property going forward, something the seller does not care about once it's out of their name. Bottom line So, as the AI trade plays out, be sure to watch trading in credit default swaps. It can get complicated, but from the perspective of stock investors, don't let that scare you and don't overthink it too much. Just remember that, just like insurance premiums, the movement in the CDS market can indicate whether perceived default risk is rising or falling, whether it is increasing or decreasing. While we don't think the rates on our names are anywhere near concerning at the moment, even as they are higher due to funding initiatives, where they go from here likely will determine the price action on the equity side. articles.title: Major earnings reports are due next week, but strong results may not be enough to quell market fears
articles.text: The third quarter earnings season has only just started, and it's expected to be strong, but investors are growing wary of the market. Around 70 S & P 500 companies are reporting next week. While that's far from the busiest week of earnings, it will give investors a sampling of results from businesses across different sectors. Tesla reports results Wednesday , after having just unveiled its long-delayed "flying car" Roadster that was developed with SpaceX. The latest earnings from a group of consumer-oriented companies including Procter & Gamble and American Express are also slated for release. Some semiconductor companies — Lam Research and Texas Instruments — are due out with results. Social media giant Meta Platforms is also on deck . When all is said and done, the latest quarter is expected to have been another strong one. As of Friday, 85% of the 46 S & P 500 companies that have reported thus far have beaten expectations. And, the broad market index is on track to post a blended earnings growth rate of 29% — a strong rate that's suspected to come in much higher by the end of the season. That would be a boon for equities, as traders hope the strength of corporate fundamentals will support what's been a bifurcated market. For the moment, the Magnificent Seven companies are doing the heavy lifting in the indexes, while the average stock is struggling. On Wednesday of this week, small caps quietly fell into correction territory . "These conditions right now, where we have sort of a, some stocks are winning and some stocks are losing — it's not a real healthy condition for the market," said Bob Lang, chief options analyst at Explosive Options. But there are other reasons to be concerned. This week, Paul Tudor Jones said 2027 could be a really challenging year for the stock market, because of new equity supply from major tech IPOs and a ballooning U.S. fiscal deficit. Adding to the pressure is an environment of higher interest rates, with oil remaining elevated and the upward pressure in bond yields. Last night, traders listening to Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh speak at an IMF event in Bangkok came away with the notion that the central bank will keep rates steady at the end of this month. But rate expectations remain elevated also, according to fed funds futures pricing, with the potential for even two hikes coming by the end of December. There's also the worry that there will soon be a deceleration in the artificial intelligence spending cycle, which is going to shape what parts of the market do better and worse. That's part of the reason that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) was down for a ninth straight day on Friday, a streak that hasn't occurred since 2006. Earnings, also, appear to be peaking. While the S & P 500 is expected to post strong growth this season, most of it is driven by energy and tech. Without those two sectors, earnings for the rest of the S & P 500 are expected to have slowed to 7% in the third quarter from 12% in the second, according to Bank of America this week. The bull market turned four just this week, a milestone that historically suggests further gains ahead, even if they're more muted. However, worries around rates, AI spending and the sustainability of strong earnings could pressure the stock market enough that a pullback of 5% may be on its way by the end of the year, Lang said. More importantly, those factors could also cloud the stock market outlook next year. "We're not going to have these strong growth rates in revenue and earnings for stocks for forever," Lang said. "We're not going to grow 20% to 30% every quarter the rest of our days here. So, eventually things [are] going to slow down a little bit." "And if the cost of money continues to be expensive, just continue to rise, then eventually it's going to be a backlash for the rest of the economy," he added. Week ahead calendar All times ET. articles.title: Wall Street's fear gauge is ripping. Traders see it going even higher
articles.text:
The sell-off in AI-related stocks pushed the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) above 22 for the first time in four months. A cluster of trades suggests it could go even higher.
In a series of eyebrow raising trades, investors purchased a number of November VIX calls that payoff if the index stays elevated through November. Specifically, one trader bought 9200 of the November 18, 20-strike calls for $1.7 million and 12,500 of the November 18, 23-strike calls for $1.1 million, wagering that the VIX will close above 23 by the third week of November.
"The speed at which VIX increased today, combined with elevated VIX options volume suggests traders are actively monetizing October VIX positions and rolling to hedge a larger market downturn. We note several +$1 million call VIX prints for November," said Brent Kochuba, founder of SpotGamma and a CNBC contributor.
Cracks in the AI complex and fears around neo-cloud provider CoreWeave caused the Nasdaq to shed 2%, its worst day since June 5th. CoreWeave lost 13%.
Of the top ten most popular VIX contracts to buy in Friday's session, nine were calls, and six were at strikes above where the VIX fell to after its initial spike. Nearly $27M in premium was traded across those nine contracts, or just about 36% of the total premium traded in VIX options on the day.
The market faces a key test next week when Tesla, SpaceX and Meta report earnings.

articles.title: Looking for a non-AI trade? This bank stock is poised for a breakout next week
articles.text: (See the video above for Jay's complete chart breakdown.) As a former market maker at the NYSE, one of the drawbacks was that I had to trade the same stocks every single day. articles.title: Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test
articles.text:
Apple's iPhone Duo, its most expensive iPhone ever, went up for preorder Friday, with launch-day pickup inventory selling out and some online delivery estimates already slipping into late January.
The company said in a statement that the preorder demand was "nothing short of extraordinary."
"We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online," Apple said.
Apple's first foldable phone starts at $1,999 and passes $3,000 at the 2TB storage tier. It is the biggest change to the physical design of the iPhone in years and establishes an entirely new price point above the Pro and Pro Max.
The early rush offers a first glimpse at the demand behind Apple's bet: Whether a dramatic new design can persuade customers to spend more and push the iPhone even further as a status symbol.
But analysts who spoke with CNBC said Apple's bet is not that foldables suddenly become a mass-market product. It is that a relatively small group of its highest-spending customers can become significantly more valuable.
Foldables are expected to make up just over 2% of global smartphone units this year but nearly 7% of industry revenue, according to IDC. By 2030, IDC expects the category to account for 10% of smartphone revenue while still representing only about 3% of units.
That gap between volume and value is central to Apple's opportunity.
"Duo is fast becoming an aspirational foldable," IDC's Nabila Popal told CNBC, comparing its appeal with Apple's broader position as an aspirational smartphone brand.
Popal, global senior research director for the Consumer Device Team at IDC, said the technology itself is not necessarily the breakthrough. Foldable Android phones have existed for years. What's new is Apple bringing that form factor to the enormous base of consumers already invested in the iPhone ecosystem.
Apple itself has been exploring the form factor for more than a decade. In 2011, Ternus and five other Apple engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, according to a recent Time profile.
"It's not that it's a breakthrough or new technology, but it's from Apple," Popal said.
The Duo could also prove more accessible than some industry watchers had anticipated.
Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights who attended Apple's launch event, said many expected the foldable iPhone to start between $2,400 and $2,500.
Apple coming in at $1,999, Sag said, suggests the company "wants a lot of share."
Sag expects the Duo to become "very much a status symbol" during the holiday season and potentially into next year.
That status appeal could be reinforced by scarcity.
Counterpoint Research Director Tarun Pathak told CNBC the firm expects initial demand to exceed supply.
Apple has an installed base of roughly 1.4 billion iPhones, he noted, meaning even a small percentage of early adopters could overwhelm the roughly 6 million or fewer units Counterpoint expects to be available in the near term.
IDC also expects supply to be constrained initially because of the complexity of the device and Apple's manufacturing and quality standards.
"Exclusivity is part of the current appeal," Popal said.
And Apple has made explicit luxury plays before.
When the first Apple Watch launched, the company offered the 18-karat gold Edition starting at $10,000. Apple also formed a long-running partnership with Hermès around premium watch bands and designs.
That push came during the tenure of Angela Ahrendts, the former Burberry CEO who joined Apple in 2014 to lead retail and online stores, as the company experimented with bringing more of the language and presentation of luxury fashion into its stores and products.
The Duo takes that idea into Apple's largest product business.
Low volume, high value
IDC expects Apple to ship roughly 7 million units this year, or roughly 3% of Apple's total shipments in 2026.
Popal, the IDC analyst, forecasts Duo shipments could grow another 70% next year. That would give Apple roughly 40% of the global foldable market and would make it the category's largest player, surpassing Samsung and Huawei. 
According to her forecast, Apple could ship as many Duos in the next six months as the previous category leaders did in all of 2025.
But the more important number for Apple may not be units.
A large share of Duo customers are expected to be existing iPhone owners, analysts said, including consumers who otherwise might have purchased a Pro Max and are now trading up to a device costing hundreds of dollars more.
Others could add the Duo as a second smartphone, with Apple's ecosystem allowing users to move relatively seamlessly between it and their primary iPhone.
Popal said that migration from roughly $1,200 premium iPhones to a device starting at nearly $2,000 should provide a "healthy boost" to Apple's revenue even if overall volumes remain relatively small.
JPMorgan reached a similar conclusion.
The bank expects the Duo to have a disproportionate impact on iPhone revenue because of its much higher average selling price, even as overall iPhone shipments are expected to remain roughly flat next year.
JPMorgan said the iPhone 18 cycle is increasingly likely to be driven by price and product mix rather than unit growth.
D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said Apple needs the Duo to succeed as it comes up against a difficult set of earnings comps with its strongest upgrade cycle in years.
"Without an uplift from Duo, they may experience some pretty pedestrian revenue growth," Luria told CNBC.
The device gives Apple several ways to generate that uplift, he added.
It raises the company's average selling price by capturing die-hard Apple customers who might otherwise have bought a Pro Max. It could bring in some consumers who previously bought folding Android phones because Apple did not offer one. And it could create a halo around the rest of the iPhone lineup.
Luria said some consumers will visit Apple stores specifically to see the Duo, "but probably walk out with an iPhone or iPhone Pro at half the price."
That means the Duo can potentially help Apple even when someone decides not to buy it.
Lead times for the iPhone 18 Pro have softened in several markets compared with the prior cycle, while the more expensive Pro Max has held up better, according to JPMorgan's tracking.
Morgan Stanley has separately said its supply-chain checks are consistent with unusually early component order reductions for the Pro and Pro Max, though the firm has not yet seen evidence that those adjustments have translated into cuts to finished iPhone production.
That puts more pressure on the Duo to pull buyers toward the very top of Apple's lineup.
Pushing the iPhone upmarket
Apple's move toward a more expensive iPhone comes as the economics of the broader smartphone market become increasingly difficult.
Consumers are already holding on to phones for longer, and global smartphone growth is slowing.
Wayne Lam, an analyst at TechInsights, said moving the iPhone further upmarket gives Apple another way to protect the revenue generated by its most important product.
"Given that the iPhone is almost 20 years old, there really isn't anywhere else to head to, given Apple's market position," Lam told CNBC.
With smartphone sales expected to slow, he said, "moving upmarket allows Apple to maintain the all-important iPhone revenues they report every quarter."
Lam described the Duo as an aspirational or luxury product rather than something designed for the average consumer.
But unlike Apple's Vision products, he believes the foldable phone has a path toward becoming a larger category over time, particularly as artificial intelligence changes how consumers interact with their devices.
The trade-off is that pushing prices higher could also make consumers wait longer to upgrade.
Higher iPhone prices could stretch already-long upgrade cycles even further, Lam said, creating what he described as a potential negative feedback loop: devices become more expensive, consumers hold on to them longer and overall demand falls.
Still, Lam expects demand for the Duo to be high relative to its initially limited supply and said the device could "set the bar for premium iPhones moving forward."

articles.title: We're downgrading this retail stock after a big comeback. Plus, AI names slide again
articles.text: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. Wall Street is selling off Friday, wrapping up what's been a volatile week for stocks. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down about 2.2%, followed by a 1.2% decline for the S & P 500 . The blue-chip Dow is down about 300 points, or 0.6%. Working against the market on Friday was WTI crude 's climb back to $100 per barrel and an uptick in Treasury yields. Although the S & P 500 is only down 2% from the record close it set on Oct. 6, AI-related technology and infrastructure stocks are under significant pressure on concerns about the rising cost of capital to fund the data center buildout and slowing revenue growth at Anthropic. The iShares Semiconductor ETF , or SOXX, is down another 3% on Friday and has now pulled back about 15% since its last positive day on Oct. 5. Club names Intel , Nvidia , Micron , and Broadcom are four of the five biggest positions in the SOXX. We aren't ready to add to these names just yet, as Jim Cramer said on Thursday's Monthly Meeting, but we're keeping an eye on levels where bearishness looks too extreme in the face of still strong demand. The market also came for the once-high-flying cybersecurity stocks this week, with CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks among some of the biggest decliners in the portfolio. While tech faltered, the market rotated into defensive consumer staples like Kimberly-Clark , healthcare like Eli Lilly and Cardinal Health , and other year-to-date laggards. In the case of Kimberly-Clark, it wasn't just rotational dynamics that lifted shares higher. A bunch of things went right for the maker of Kleenex and Huggies, including two regulatory approvals for the Kenvue acquisition and the release of better-than-feared preliminary results for its third quarter. TJX Companies was one of the bright spots this week, with shares rallying about 5%. But in keeping with our comments during Thursday's Monthly Meeting, we are formally downgrading our rating on TJX to a hold-equivalent 2 after this big run. Sure, the off-price retailer's stock is still down about $3 from where it traded before the company in August reported a big slowdown in its TJ Maxx and Marshalls division. As disappointing as this was, we thought the slowdown was self-inflicted and fixable, which is why we stuck with the stock and added to our position three times as it slid from $140 to $138 and all the way down to $125 . We kept buying because we simply did not understand why the market ignored management's comments about an improved August, and we're glad to see the market come around to our view. But the stock's rebound from its lows to $147 on Friday — combined with our steady buying — has pushed our TJX position size to about 4.25%. Accordingly, we would take profits Friday to right-size the position if we weren't restricted from trading it. Earnings season picks up next week , although only two companies in the portfolio are scheduled to report. On Tuesday, we'll see earnings from Capital One after the closing bell, and Meta Platforms reports Wednesday night. Beyond those names, we'll see earnings from a handful of industrials like 3M , GE Aerospace , RTX , Lockheed Martin , General Motors , and ex-Club name Honeywell Technologies . Tesla reports too. Within technology, IBM , Lam Research , Western Digital , and Texas Instruments report. A bunch of airlines and railroad operators also fill the earnings calendar, so we'll be watching how higher fuel prices are impacting profits. Rounding things out are a bunch of regional banks, American Express , Netflix , Procter & Gamble , and oilfield services companies SLB and Halliburton . On the economic data side, it's thankfully a bit lighter with no jobs or inflation data. Nevertheless, we'll see housing starts, building permits, October S & P Global U.S. Manufacturing and Services PMI, and the University of Michigan's survey on consumer sentiment and one-year inflation expectations. articles.title: Trump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in Ukraine
articles.text:
President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces.
Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."
Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
Ukrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour.
Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions."
Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote. "As your European customers, we are watching you."
Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian.
The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions.
Reuters reported on Thursday, citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order.
On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far."
Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.
SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday.

articles.title: Yields continue to rattle investors. These sectors are most at risk if rates stay elevated
articles.text: U.S. Treasury yields have been volatile as of late, putting certain rate-sensitive industries at risk while others hold up, market strategists and investors told CNBC. The 10-year Treasury yield has surged more than 90 basis points in 2026 and hit a 2002 high above 5.3% earlier this month. The 30-year Treasury bond yield also scaled to 24-year highs in October, briefly topping 5.7%. And while yields have pulled back from those levels, they could sail higher again as new inflation data raises questions about whether the Federal Reserve will have to raise rates further to stave off pricing pressures. On Wednesday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported consumer prices rose 3.7% in September on a year-over-year basis, above Wall Street's expectations. That's led traders to price in at least one more Fed rate hike before year-end, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Higher rates can complicate the investment outlook for several sectors — such as homebuilders and utilities. Companies in these spaces tend to have elevated debt loads and are involved in capital-intensive businesses. However, healthcare is one area of the market that is likely to remain resilient in a high-rate environment. "Equities are going to be choppy," said Gregory Faranello, head of macro strategy at South Street Securities. "When you hit pockets like this, it pays just to take a step back and think a little bit and say, 'what are the key risk buckets here?'" Susceptible stocks Homebuilders are likely to suffer if Treasury yields remain elevated. In September, 38% of builders slashed their prices, up from 35% in August, as they contended with sluggish demand due to rising mortgage rates, according to the latest National Association of Home Builders /Wells Fargo Housing Market Index. The iShares U.S. Home Construction ETF (ITB) dropped 7.3% last month, as rates climbed. That marked its worst monthly performance since July, when it tumbled 9.7%. "Homebuilders is an industry that's going to continue to get hurt by higher mortgage rates reducing the affordability of housing," said Raymond James CIO Larry Adam. "That's one area that will be very susceptible." Utilities could also struggle in a higher-rate environment due to their heavy investments and relatively high debt loads, per Bill Northey, senior investment director at U.S. Bank Asset Management Group. "You have a little bit more cyclicality and higher degrees of operating leverage, so those are going to be a little bit more vulnerable to [higher rates]," Northey told CNBC. The S & P 500 utilities sector fell more than 6% in September, its biggest monthly drop since December 2024. Back then, it tumbled 8.7%. The sector is also down around 1% in 2026, while the S & P 500 has climbed 12%. Technology stocks are also poised to slide if rates continue to climb — particularly as investors raise concerns over the feasibility of the artificial intelligence data center expansion, according to Northey. AI stocks are declining as investors' fears over the extent of technology companies' borrowing for the AI buildout intensifies. In September, cloud stock CoreWeave stoked jitters after it sold more than $4 billion in convertible bonds. Its total debt now stands at more than $51 billion . Tech stocks and other long-duration assets with high valuations "demonstrate some degree of vulnerability," Northey said. "When you have rapid move-in rates like we've seen over the course of the past six weeks, that's where you can see some degree of influence around equity pricing." The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) is on track to end its ninth consecutive session in the red, marking its most prolonged losing streak in years. More broadly, small caps — whether in technology or another sector — are particularly vulnerable to higher rates, according to Raymond James' Adam. Small caps have languished in correction territory amid broader market volatility. The Russell 2000 is down more than 11% from a record high reached in August. It's an "area that will continue to have a major headwind in front of them," the investor said. "Roughly about 54% of their debt financing is done with short-term debt. So, a rise in interest rates really has a bigger impact on their financing." Resilient part of the market Healthcare could weather the storm better than many other stocks, however. That's because healthcare companies demonstrate steady earnings and consistent, non-cyclical demand, according to U.S. Bank's Northey. While he did not provide specific names, CNBC Pro screened FactSet for healthcare stocks that are well liked on the Street. Specifically, we filtered for names that were in the S & P 500 healthcare sector with buy ratings from at least 55% of analysts and upside to an average price target of 10% or more. Abbott Laboratories made the list with 65% of analysts rating the stock a buy. The average analyst target also implies upside of nearly 16% from Thursday's close. The stock is up nearly 6% over the past three months. Boston Scientific and CVS Health also made the cut.

articles.title: The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis
articles.text:
In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.
For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.
With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.
The credit market slow moving steamroller
The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.
From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:
- Bond Swoon: Bonds issued at par just this past June at an 8.5% rate fell nearly 18% through last Friday, following a severe initial swoon in late July.
- CDS Spikes: 5-year Credit Default Swaps (CDS) exploded from 452 bps in early June to over 1100 bps this week, implying a roughly 60% probability of default within the next five years.
- Cash Flow Burn: The company faces an estimated $16.45 billion in negative free cash flow in the second half of this year alone, and another $30.6 billion in FY2027, according to Bloomberg
- Cost of Capital: With a 15% cost of capital, the structural hurdle rate for new business is staggering. Even with optimistic pricing power through 2028, forecast Debt/EBITDA at FYE2028 sits at 4.5x, which warrants caution, and only if the company hits all those ambitious numbers.
Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.
The sell-side tug of war
Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.
It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.
The Trade: November 80/January 72.5 call diagonal
With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.
Structure Mechanics:
- Buy the January 72.5 Calls pay $10.25
- Sell the November 80 Calls @ $4.30
