articles.title: Companies hint at layoffs, without saying who or when—and employees are left wondering who's on the chopping block
articles.text:
As companies hint at layoffs ahead without sharing specifics, employees are left wondering who will be on the chopping block — and when.
Nike CEO Elliott Hill said on Oct. 1 that changes to its operating model "will result in fewer roles," with decisions on impacted roles coming in "2027 and beyond." Following the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger, Skydance CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz wrote that such deals "bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce." On Oct. 12, Kroger CEO Greg Foran told staff of plans to cut 3,000 corporate jobs over the next three years as "technology is reshaping what's possible."
Word of coming layoffs, in some cases months or years out, can hurt productivity and spur worker anxiety in the absence of a timeline or more concrete information. It could also help win over investors and give employees a head start to head out.
Announcing cuts without specifying who will be affected or when is a departure from the norm: Often, companies alert affected employees on the day that will be their last, says Denise Rousseau, professor of organizational behavior and public policy at Carnegie Mellon University. But that approach is "very dysfunctional" and "really destructive of both reputation and employee well-being," she adds.
A bigger heads-up causes "a lot more anxiety than a sudden dropping of the hammer," Rousseau adds, although it "does give employees more options."
Why companies are warning workers about layoffs early
Layoff announcements with long runways could be a play to appeal to investors.
"It's a way of saying to the investors, 'We understand we're going to have to change, and we're going to try to get on this as soon as we can,'" says Peter Cappelli, management professor and director of the Center for Human Resources at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School.
Internally, companies could have different motivations.
They may hope to save on severance costs by scaring some employees into leaving on their own rather than waiting to be let go. But it often doesn't work that way: "You're not going to scare the people who are not good performers because it's hard for them to get a job someplace else," Cappelli says. So employers risk losing their star employees, who can more easily find other jobs.
To try to combat this, employers may offer retention bonuses or other incentives to high performers or other employees in roles critical to the restructure, Rousseau says.
Across the board, the consequences for workers can be severe. "It's a huge distraction for the workforce," Rousseau says. "It makes people stressed, and you probably don't get their best contributions because of that."
Some companies could be trying to "scare employees into working hard" to try to keep their jobs, Cappelli said. "There are business leaders who think that's the way you motivate people." But that's not an effective tactic, the professors say.
What this means for workers
Some workers, particularly lower performers, may opt to "hunker down and hide," Cappelli says. Others may turn to "loud working," angling for hypervisibility at work to try to avoid being laid off. But that won't necessarily help workers keep their jobs, Cappelli and Rousseau say, and can instead fuel burnout, especially if workers are doing it for months or years before companies reveal the specifics of the job cuts.
For employees hearing of planned job cuts, it wouldn't hurt to look out for opportunities elsewhere, the professors say, even though slow hiring in the U.S. right now can be discouraging.
It may be some consolation, they add, that employers' plans are also likely to change over the long time frames. Cuts may not happen in the way the companies are planning now, Cappelli says: "They don't have any idea what things are going to look like in three years."
"There's a lot of uncertainty," Rousseau adds. "You don't know how the environment will react, what the price of diesel will be, what the supply chains will be like."

articles.title: Debt is eating up a bigger chunk of your raise, research shows
articles.text:
A version of this article first appeared in ″CNBC's Money 101 Newsletter with Sharon Epperson,″ an eight-week series with monthly updates to help improve your financial well-being. Subscribe now to receive the series in your inbox. It is also available in Spanish.
Consumer spending has helped keep the U.S. economy resilient. Yet research shows debt payments are taking a growing bite out of Americans' income gains, leaving less money available to spend or save.
A new analysis by the nonpartisan think tank The Century Foundation and the consumer advocacy group Protect Borrowers found that a typical U.S. household's estimated real take-home monthly pay rose $109 from late 2022 to early 2026. "Real" take-home pay is one's wage after accounting for inflation.
Meanwhile, a worker's monthly debt payments rose $57.
In other words, researchers estimate that for a one-earner household, 52 cents of every dollar of income gained in recent years goes to higher debt payments. For a two-earner household, they project that the entire real income gain, and then some, goes toward debt.
The analysis also found inflation-adjusted debt payments rose nearly 15% over roughly three years — about eight times as fast as household income, which grew less than 2%.
Household debt squeeze
The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers analyzed credit records for millions of working-age Americans ages 25 to 64, along with Census Bureau income data. The research includes payments on credit cards, auto loans and leases, student loans and home equity lines of credit. It excludes mortgages and some other borrowing, including many buy now, pay later loans and medical payment plans.
Angela Hanks, chief of policy programs at The Century Foundation, said the findings may understate the financial pressure households face.
"Even though it shows that workers' wages are getting eaten up by debt payments at a tremendous level," Hanks said, the findings represent "perhaps the rosiest analysis that we could have done using the data."
She said adding mortgage payments as well as installment loans not included in a credit file — like buy now, pay later and payday loans — would have made household debt payments higher.
More consumers are relying on credit cards to cover basic expenses when their paychecks fall short, she said.
Separate Federal Reserve data underscores the strain. The Fed's latest Survey of Consumer Finances found 8.6% of families spent more than 40% of their income on debt payments in 2025, up from 6.5% in 2022 — a level not seen since the 2013 survey.
Avoid the debt trap
Mortgages and student loans are often considered "good debt" because they may help build wealth or earning power. But even potentially beneficial debt, or debt taken on for necessary expenses, can become a financial burden.
"When that debt stretches out for six months or a year or longer, or if you're taking out a seven-year auto loan, or if you're taking out a longer mortgage than maybe you ideally would want to, or a bigger mortgage, that's when things get a little dicey," said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree and author of "Ask Questions, Save Money, Make More."
To avoid taking on more debt than you can afford, he recommends three simple steps:
- Set a budget. Know how much you can realistically spend before you borrow or shop.
- Make a list. Shop with specific purchases in mind rather than giving in to impulse buys.
- Compare prices. Shopping around can reduce costs and how much you may need to borrow.
Before taking on debt, consider the total borrowing cost, repayment terms and whether you have enough savings to handle unexpected expenses, Schulz said.
— CNBC's Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting.

articles.title: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year
articles.text:
The U.S. finished the 2026 fiscal year with a budget deficit of nearly $2 trillion, the latest measurement to underscore the extent of the country's financial stress.
The $1.992 trillion figure was about 12% higher than the $1.775 trillion deficit in the prior fiscal year, the Treasury Department reported Friday.
It's the third-highest annual deficit in U.S. history, behind only 2020 and 2021, when the federal government was doling out trillions of dollars in financial stimulus amid the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2026 fiscal year saw record sums for both receipts and outlays, according to a Treasury Department official.
With Friday's release, the U.S. officially recorded its 25th straight fiscal year operating at a deficit. The government last recorded a surplus — meaning its revenues were larger than debts — in 2001.
Friday's report offers fresh evidence of how the U.S.'s fast-growing debt pile has dragged on the nation's overall financial health. The rising debt bill has helped exacerbate angst among bond traders, who sent the 10-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury yields to 24-year highs last week.
Where the debt comes from
Social Security amounted to the biggest slice of government spending at nearly $1.7 trillion for the full fiscal year, up modestly from the roughly $1.6 trillion spent in 2025.
Medicare was the second biggest contributor, costing almost $1.1 trillion for the fiscal year. By comparison, the government-run healthcare program required slightly under $1 trillion in fiscal 2025.
Net interest – a calculation of the Treasury's gross interest minus the interest it receives – also topped $1 trillion for the fiscal year. In the 2025 fiscal year, net interest totaled $970 billion.
Individual incomes taxes helped lessen the total deficit by bringing in more than $2.8 trillion, an increase of about 7% year over year. Corporate income tax provided $381 billion in receipts during the 2026 fiscal year. That was a decrease of about $70 billion from fiscal 2025 stemming from the tax cuts included in the One Big Beautiful Bill act passed by Congress last year.
In the 2026 fiscal year, the U.S. shelled out more than $1.3 trillion in interest on the national public debt. The total owed exceeded $40 trillion earlier this year and has more than doubled over the last decade.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC in August that the U.S. can "grow our way out of" its increasing debt pile.
"Our message to our allies, our trading partners, is that global growth is the way to take care of this mountain of debt," Bessent said in August.
President Donald Trump pitched his plans for broad and steep tariffs as a way to drive up revenue and shrink the government's debt. The White House has pushed forward with its strategy of increasing levies on trading partners despite the Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that many of those instituted by Trump were unconstitutional.
The Treasury saw a record high for gross customs duties in the 2026 fiscal year, according to a department official. But the total revenue from customs took a hit due to refunds required following the Supreme Court ruling, which sent billions of dollars back to retailers.
The Treasury also reported Friday that September's monthly deficit came in at $27 billion, a reversal from the prior year, when the department saw a surplus of $198 billion in the month.

articles.title: NBA tightens betting rules, develops AI to flag suspicious wagers
articles.text:
The NBA is upping the ante when it comes to monitoring sports betting ahead of the 2026-2027 season.
The league is tightening restrictions on bets offered by its authorized gambling partners and deploying artificial intelligence to help identify suspicious wagering, according to two documents obtained by CNBC.
The measures come as Commissioner Adam Silver pushes for greater access to wagering data and more control over the types of markets offered on the league's games. He said his concerns extend to prediction markets.
"For us, whether it's called a prediction market, whether it's sports betting, it's the same issues for our league, and I think for all the leagues," Silver told CNBC last week in Macao. "There's issues around integrity first and foremost."
In the letter sent to sports betting companies including FanDuel, DraftKings, Fanatics and others, the NBA has placed restrictions on wagers on which player scores the first basket, wagers on players expected to play less than 12 minutes per game and parlays combining multiple bets on the same player's underperformance.
Those types of bets can raise integrity concerns because a single player has the ability to influence the outcome.
The changes follow a series of gambling-related cases involving NBA figures including former players Jontay Porter, Terry Rozier, and Damon Jones and former coach and player Chauncey Billups.
AI monitoring
A separate memo sent Friday to team presidents, general managers, integrity officers and lawyers says the NBA has developed an internal AI-based monitoring platform. The system analyzes basketball data, injury reports, social media information about player availability and individual betting data.
The platform is designed to help the league “promptly identify and investigate potentially suspicious betting activity,” according to the memo from Dan Spillane, the NBA’s executive vice president of league governance and policy.
Silver’s comments underscore the importance the league places on obtaining that information.
“So we want access to that data. We also want control over the markets,” Silver told CNBC.
Increasing education and training
The league is also increasing its training and education around sports betting. The memo said that former NFL player and retired FBI agent Charles Tillman, will provide in-person training to each team.
The league said it has also added new training around sports betting to NBA rookies who will now receive training at the NBA Combine and during the required Rookie Transition program.
The letter also highlights steps the league is taking to better protect players and personnel from harassment and threats by sports bettors.
As betting has become more widespread, some bettors have taken to social media to harass players for their game performance that may be tied to a bet.
To address this, the league has updated its NBA Fan Code of Conduct to highlight the prohibition on betting-related harassment.
The league is also partnering with a third-party service provider to help monitor and control harassing messages. It has also launched a new text message-based hotline to securely report threats.
The memo does not specify how the restrictions would apply to prediction market platforms.
In Macao, Silver said that he's in favor of a national framework when it comes to federal regulation around sports betting.
"We have roughly 40 different judications regulating us right now so to have a consistent policy nationally, I think would be in our best interest," he said.

articles.title: Brent oil touches $110 as Iran escalates Hormuz attacks, Ukraine vows to hit Russian refineries
articles.text:
Crude oil prices rose sharply Friday as Iran escalated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi militants fired missiles at Saudi Arabia and Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries.
Brent futures hit a session high of $110 per barrel for the first time since May before easing slightly to close at $109.86, a gain of 3.7%.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.5% to settle at $101.41 per barrel. WTI added more than 10% this week while Brent advanced nearly 5%.
Saudi Arabia intercepted several missiles fired over the Red Sea on Friday, including one that was heading toward the oil export terminal Yanbu, a military spokesman said. Three drones were also destroyed in the kingdom's Riyadh and southern regions, the military said.
Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen have repeatedly fired at Saudi Arabia this week. Oil giant Aramco came under attack when one of its administrative buildings in Dhahran was hit Tuesday, the kingdom's energy ministry said.
The Houthis attacked Riyadh's international airport on Oct. 10, killing 12 and injuring more than 300.
In the Strait of Hormuz, at least nine tankers and cargo ships have come under attack since Sunday as Iran tries to choke off oil exports through the waterway. Iran sank the container ship GFS Pride on Wednesday, U.S. Central Command said. The crew of the Singapore-registered ship was safely evacuated, according to Singapore's maritime authority.
The attacks have left three seafarers injured and two missing this week, according to the International Maritime Organization.
Crude exports through Hormuz have pulled back after touching prewar levels in September. Shipments stood at 9.4 million barrels per day for the week ended Wednesday, about 70% of the average before the Iran war, according to data provided by the energy researcher Kpler.
Meanwhile, the "energy ceasefire" that President Donald Trump tried to broker between Ukraine and Russia has quickly unraveled. The Kremlin continued attacking Ukrainian infrastructure despite the supposed truce. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv would resume strikes on Russian refineries in retaliation.
Diesel prices have surged this year due to Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries and Iranian strikes on energy infrastructure in the Middle East. The fuel cost an average of $6.33 a gallon in the U.S. Friday, more than 70% above the same period last year, according to AAA data.
U.S. crude oil prices were also driven higher by a big decline of more than 8 million barrels for the week ended Oct. 9 in commercial inventories due to production shut-ins on the Gulf Coast from Hurricane Isaias, according to the Energy Information Administration.

articles.title: Katie Zacharia out as Trump's White House press secretary
articles.text:
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job after just five days in the face of criticism over her performance, a White House official confirmed to CNBC on Friday.
Earlier Friday afternoon, President Donald Trump told reporters that he had just suggested to Zacharia that she quit.
"I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump said outside the White House.
"'If I were you, I'd reconsider,'" the president said he told Zacharia.
The White House official, who asked not to be named in order to discuss the staffing shake-up, confirmed Fox News' report that Zacharia is "transitioning" out of the press secretary role.
Zacharia's five-day tenure in the Trump administration is shorter than that of Anthony Scaramucci, who in 2017 served as White House communications director for less than 11 days. That length of time became jokingly referred to as a "Scaramucci" and was used to measure the durations of other officials who served briefly.
By that metric, Zacharia lasted one-half of one Scaramucci.
"Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain," Scaramucci said in an X post later Friday.
Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked at Trump Media & Technology Group, had faced widespread criticism in the days since she led a short and shaky first press briefing. She also came under mounting scrutiny about her legal background.
Trump spoke to reporters before heading to Georgia for a political rally as he hopes to boost Republicans' electoral chances with just 18 days until the midterms.
But Trump's efforts to sell his agenda have been muddled in part by Zacharia, who ended her first, and only, press briefing on Tuesday after delivering halting remarks and taking questions from just three reporters.
In the less than six minutes she spent answering questions, Zacharia revealed that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to step down. That departure, and Zacharia's, follow those of a number of other high-ranking female officials in the Trump administration who have quit or been fired in recent months.
"You know, she's been treated very rough. And she's a nice person," Trump said of Zacharia outside the White House.
He accused the media of treating her "very badly" and said that even Fox News TV host Sean Hannity, a supporter of the administration, was "a little bit tough" on Zacharia during her appearance on his show Thursday night.
Hannity, after calling Zacharia's debut briefing "widely panned," had asked about her past claims about her legal work in light of reports that she never passed a bar exam. Zacharia has defended identifying herself as a lawyer, drawing a distinction between that label and calling herself an "attorney."
Hannity pointed out that Zacharia had called herself an attorney in multiple social media posts. "I think they were retweets, and I corrected the record," she replied.
Trump called Zacharia "an attorney" in his Oct. 9 Truth Social post announcing her selection to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in late August. Zacharia's first day was Columbus Day.
White House officials had defended Zacharia earlier this week. "Up and down the White House, everyone has been thoroughly impressed with Katie in just a few short days on the job," White House communications director Steven Cheung said in an X post Wednesday.
"At the end of this second term, she'll be remembered as one of the all-time greats," Cheung wrote.
CNN chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins, however, reported Friday that Trump was "embarrassed by the coverage of Zacharia's briefing and when he polled other aides about her, Zacharia had few allies willing to stand up for her or defend her performance."
"She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily," Trump said of Zacharia in Friday's remarks outside the White House. "And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want.'"
Asked if he would keep her in the role, Trump said, "I'm going to let her make that decision."

articles.title: Here's who Netflix just brought in to run content — and what it means for the streamer
articles.text:
Netflix is shaking up its C-suite in an effort to fix its engagement woes.
On Thursday, the streaming giant announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice will take over as the company's chief content officer, overseeing global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events.
Rice is replacing 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria, who most recently led the company's global content team with a focus on its live sports strategy. Bajaria was initially hired in 2016 to help the streamer launch an unscripted division as well as licensing and studio co-productions. She later transitioned to the top creative role, spearheading Netflix's $20 billion content budget.
She oversaw popular TV series like "Stranger Things," "Wednesday," "Bridgerton," "Squid Game," "Adolescence" and "Beef," as well as Netflix films like "Frankenstein" and "KPop Demon Hunters." Bajaria also helped push Netflix into live sports and events, including deals with the WWE and the NFL as well as programs like "The Roast of Tom Brady."
Prior to his stint at Disney, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group as well as Fox's lead executive on the Hulu board. He was also the president of Fox Searchlight Pictures and helped release "Slumdog Millionaire," "Juno," "Little Miss Sunshine" and "Sideways."
The executive change follows a tumultuous period for Netflix as it faces stagnating viewership and explores avenues for growth. It comes just days after the streaming giant laid off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce.
The last time Netflix made cuts of this size was in 2022 when it reported its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than 10 years.
"We believe this round of layoffs reflects more structural changes to the cost base than a reaction to near-term subscriber dynamics," wrote Brian Pitz, managing director and head of internet and interactive entertainment equity research at BMO Capital Markets, in a research note published Friday.
Flagging engagement
In July, Netflix reported viewership increased just 2% in the first half of the year as the streamer suffers from a lack of shows with water-cooler-level hype.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted last month during the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company is "not growing as fast as I want us to."
Those warnings, and now Bajaria's exit, have Wall Street bracing for more turbulence ahead.
"The sudden departure of Bajaria likely signals to us that user engagement may have remained soft throughout [the third quarter]," Pitz wrote.
Netflix is set to release fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.
In July, Nielsen reported that Netflix had generated 7.8% of TV viewership, while YouTube accounted for nearly double that, at 14.2%.
YouTube has been Netflix's biggest threat in the battle for viewers' time. In response, the streaming giant has sought to diversify its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention.
"If the opportunity is to recast [Netflix] into a broader content hub, the risk is missing the watercooler originals," Steven Cahall, equity analyst at Wells Fargo, wrote in a research note last month. "We see breakout hits as a must for the stock to work again."
What Rice brings to Netflix
Rice has a wealth of experience in television and film, most recently serving as the chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the company. He managed a wide swath of channels across broadcast and streaming, including ABC, Disney Channel, Hulu and FX Networks. During his tenure, he oversaw the production of more than 300 shows, including "American Idol," "Modern Family," "Abbott Elementary," "The Bear," "Only Murders in the Building" and "Shogun."
He also headed up major sporting events such as coverage of the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup.
Under Rice's leadership, Disney earned roughly 300 Primetime Emmy nominations between 2021 and 2022. Of those nods, it won nearly 60 awards across its television networks and streaming platforms.
Meanwhile, Netflix's Emmy wins have slowed.
In 2021, it tied the record for most trophies won by an outlet in a single year with 44. This year, however, it only took home 16 prizes, its lowest Emmy haul in a decade.
With Rice, Netflix is also getting an executive with theatrical experience. After he was ousted by then-Disney CEO Bob Chapek in mid-2022, he transitioned into an independent producer role. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later." He's currently developing a movie adaptation of the video game "Elden Ring."
Late last year, Netflix struck a deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery's film studio and streaming assets, only to be outbid months later by Paramount Skydance, which completed its acquisition of WBD in early October.
Some on Wall Street have speculated that the streamer may be interested in further M&A, including acquiring assets from NBCUniversal after it splits from parent company Comcast.
"[Rice's] long tenure at Fox, and then Disney after its acquisition of Fox, gives him unique insight into the consolidation of two major studios, relevant if Netflix chooses to go after another studio," Alicia Reese, senior vice president of equity research at Wedbush, wrote in a research note Thursday. "Even if it doesn't, Rice's experience fits well as Netflix pushes deeper into theatrical and builds a broader platform with varied content across the entertainment ecosystem."

articles.title: The drumbeat to buy battered shares of CoreWeave is growing louder on Wall Street
articles.text: The artificial intelligence trade tanked this week as Anthropic reported decelerating revenue growth amid accelerating AI capex, adding fuel to the fire of a sell-off in the AI-dedicated server companies known as neoclouds – especially CoreWeave . Analysts are perking up about CoreWeave, even though investors are dumping shares and interest rates are rising in the economy. The stock is down about 11% as of 12:38 p.m. ET, while the 2032 bond yield is flat. CRWV 1D mountain CRWV 1 day Analyst Brent Thill at Jefferies described the sell-off as "overdone" in a note to investors. He reiterated his price target of $150, suggesting upside of 115% from Thursday's close. Thill said that CoreWeave's pricing power is increasing even as its debt service costs may expand. "Higher rates on future deals are a fair risk... With rising yields on CRWV's unsecured debt and higher rates broadly, the market is increasingly worried about CRWV's future cost of capital. It's a valid concern that new debt deals could price at higher rates. ...but pricing for capacity is rising much faster in the near term," Thill wrote in his analysis. Falling expectations for an interest rate increase at the Federal Reserve's next meeting later this month may be giving CoreWeave bonds some room to breathe. The odds of a quarter-point rate hike have dropped to just 17% in futures markets , as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh declined to give a rate signal in his latest public appearance. In a Friday note to clients, JPMorgan also asserted that fears were "overdone" while touting CoreWeave's fundamentals. The firm rates the stock overweight. "Datacenter demand is robust and has improved in recent months, rather than moderated," Samik Chatterjee at JPMorgan wrote. The analyst also noted that CoreWeave's "capacity is pre-sold under long-term take-or-pay contracts rather than building for estimated demand." However, other analysts have expressed concerns about assuming that take-or-pay legal structures are iron-clad and about equating backlogs with revenue. Attorneys who specialize in the field are anticipating disputes over the contractual framework in the future. Other neoclouds in addition to CoreWeave are also down, with Nebius falling 9% and IREN falling 8% in midday trading Friday. NBIS 1D mountain NBIS 1 day Analysts at Cantor Fitzgerald said that "false narratives [are running] amok" on CoreWeave in a Thursday note to clients amid the rise in its bond yields over 15%. "We believe this is one of the most attractive times to add to or enter into a CRWV position, as we think the market is getting it wrong," Brett Knoblauch at Cantor wrote. "We would advise investors to take a step back and look at how CRWV's business has consistently improved."

articles.title: Anything not tied to artificial intelligence took off this week
articles.text: Stocks outside the artificial intelligence trade are outperforming the broader market this week by one of the widest margins in nearly three years, according to a recent CNBC analysis of FactSet data. This week's leading S & P 500 outperformers unrelated to AI include Fair Isaac , up almost 14%, Equifax , ahead 10.4%, Darden Restaurants , 10.3% higher, and Brown-Forman , 9% to the good. The split was especially sharp on Wednesday, when the S & P ex-AI index gained 0.61%, outperforming the S & P 500 by 1.72 percentage points, and recording the fifth largest daily gap in favor of the ex-AI benchmark this year. For the week through Thursday, the S & P ex-AI index gained 2.4% while the S & P 500 index declined nearly 1%, putting the ex-AI index ahead by 3.29 percentage points, on pace for its second-biggest weekly outperformance since early 2024. Only the week ended June 26 produced a wider gap recently. Stocks outside AI rose 2.3% that week as the S & P 500 fell roughly 2%, resulting in a 4.26 percentage-point spread. Over the long term, the ex-AI benchmark still trails the S & P 500 but this week's performance offers a snapshot of gains that go beyond the companies tied to the AI hype. Investors are reassessing the market which has increasingly been influenced by a concentrated group of AI-related companies. Reflecting investor desire to look beyond the handful of largest stocks powering the market since ChatGPT debuted in late 2022, Goldman Sachs and S & P Dow Jones Indices introduced the S & P ex-AI index, known by the ticker SPXXAI, in February, Axios reported at the time . The index history was back tested to early January 2024. At its launch, AI-related companies accounted for about 45% of the S & P 500. Goldman positioned the index as a way for investors to measure or hedge against the AI trade and exclude companies with significant exposure to AI-related revenue, infrastructure or demand, including businesses tied to chips, data centers, networking and cloud computing. Trivector Research in August found potential in what it called " non-tech compounders, " companies offering rapid growth that don't rely on the AI buildout. Among those stocks were Eli Lilly , Tapestry and AbbVie . "Non-tech compounders can play an important role in portfolios if AI leadership broadens or volatility increases," Adam Parker, Trivector's founder, wrote.

articles.text:

articles.title: Why Trump and the GOP's billion-dollar midterm blitz isn’t working
articles.text:
A billion-dollar war chest was meant to be Republicans' great equalizer heading into a bleak midterm election environment defined by economic frustration, President Donald Trump's unpopularity and fallout from the war in Iran.
So far it hasn't worked.
From Labor Day through Oct. 14, GOP groups injected more than $740 million into congressional races that will determine control of Congress, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. That includes at least $220 million in spending from Trump-linked groups. Elon Musk has separately given another $276 million to Republican groups since July and helped boost the GOP's Senate Leadership Fund super PAC to a record quarter.
Yet with less than three weeks until the Nov. 3 Election Day, the spending blitz has barely moved the map. Democrats lead in FiftyPlusOne's polling averages across nine of the Senate's most competitive races — Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas — little changed from before the Republican spending spree. Minnesota was expected to be solidly blue, making its tight race a concern for Democrats.
And Republican political operatives and independent election observers CNBC spoke with say the money hasn't had the effects its magnitude would be expected to in voter sentiment.
Meanwhile, the broader battlefield continues to deteriorate for Republicans. Democrats are favored to flip the House and remain competitive in the Senate, according to the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, forcing the GOP to burn millions protecting once-safe seats while abandoning former pickup targets.
"Money is an amplifier, not a magic wand," said Neil Newhouse, partner at Republican polling firm Public Opinion Strategies. "You can buy all the airtime in the world, but if the political climate is blowing 30 miles an hour in your face, ad volume alone isn't going to turn the weather around."
Musk flooding the zone
Republicans entered the final stretch of the midterm election with unusually deep pockets.
MAGA Inc. had nearly $416 million on hand at the end of August, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Across the broader ecosystem, major Republican organizations had roughly $1 billion available, eclipsing the $579 million available for comparable Democratic groups, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings.
Then came Musk — after saying he'd be less involved in this year's election. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has given more than $276 million to Republican groups since July, including $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund Republican-boosting super PAC and more than $76 million to his own America PAC, according to figures confirmed to CNBC by an America PAC spokesperson. Musk's known federal political giving this election cycle now totals roughly $366 million, making him the largest known donor of the midterms.
And Musk is far from alone. Nine of the 10 largest individual and family donor groups this cycle are Republican-aligned, accounting for 86 cents of every dollar contributed by the top 10, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC records.
"We are watching an unprecedented concentration and scale of political influence and wealth this election cycle," said Hilary Braseth, executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonprofit, nonpartisan group that tracks campaign spending.
AdImpact projects $11.6 billion in political advertising this 2025-2026 cycle, surpassing both the 2022 midterms and the 2024 presidential election.
Paying more for less
However, the size of Republicans’ financial advantage may overstate how much advertising that money can actually buy.
That's because much of the GOP's money, particularly spending by Trump-aligned groups, has arrived late and via super PACs, which can pay far more for airtime than candidates. Federal law entitles candidates to broadcasters' lowest unit rate during the final 60 days before a general election; outside groups get no such protection.
It's an edge for Democrats whose candidates have generally outraised their Republican counterparts.
In Dallas, for example, Democrat James Talarico's campaign spent about $2.4 million on local broadcast ads from Oct. 1 through Oct. 14, enough for the average viewer to see his ads about 48 times, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. The pro-Ken Paxton Texas PAC spent about $7.8 million for roughly 81 views per viewer — more than three times as much money for only about 70% more exposure, according to the analysis.
Airtime has become so expensive that Paxton's allies have begun buying ads during national sporting events, calculating that reaching enough Texans through a national broadcast can cost less than buying across the state's local television markets, according to the Associated Press.
"R money advantage not what it appears to be on [the] surface," Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who lost to Paxton in the primary, posted on X on Oct. 5.
Across the nine key Senate battlegrounds identified by the Cook Political Report as of Oct. 1, Republicans led broadcast TV spending in seven and outspent Democrats by 26% overall through Sept. 30, yet generated only 7% more airings.
Super PACs don't face the same pricing disadvantage on digital ads, where campaigns and outside groups compete on more equal footing. But broadcast TV still dominates political spending, with AdImpact projecting it will account for 48% of the 2026 cycle total.
Little movement in political polls
But the payoff from all that spending has been harder to see in political polls.
Despite more than $113 million spent on negative advertising targeting Talarico since the Texas primary, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, a Siena College poll released Tuesday showed Talarico leading Paxton 48% to 44%, down only slightly from his 6-point lead in September.
In Michigan, after more than $87 million in attacks targeting Democrat Abdul El-Sayed this year, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, Fox News polling from late September found El-Sayed's favorable rating among registered voters up 5 points from its early August survey, while Republican Mike Rogers' fell 4 points.
Part of the challenge is diminishing returns on ads as Election Day nears. Political advertising experts tell CNBC that as campaigns repeatedly target the same small pool of persuadable voters, each additional dollar is less likely to reach someone who has not already heard the message.
"When an undecided voter has already seen 20 negative ads today, the 21st ad doesn't persuade them. It just gets tuned out," said Michael Beckel, money in politics reform director at Issue One. "Their eyes glaze over." Issue One works to reduce the influence of money in politics and has a board that includes former Democratic and Republican elected officials.
Still, some Republicans counter that top-line poll movement is the wrong barometer. They say the September cash influx helped keep vulnerable candidates competitive as the political environment deteriorated.
In Texas, Republicans spent $121.5 million on the Senate race in September, up from just $5.5 million over the previous three months, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, while Musk's America PAC added direct mail and canvassing. Republicans involved in the race said the picture could have been far worse without that support.
"The spending hasn't put Paxton ahead, but it kept a messy race and flawed candidate from becoming an unwinnable one," said a Republican operative involved in the Texas Senate race, who asked not to be named to speak candidly about the state of the contest.
Maine offers another test. Republicans have poured more than $50 million into the state to support incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, nearly twice Democratic spending, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. Since early September, FiftyPlusOne's polling average has tightened modestly, from about a 3-point advantage for Democrat Troy Jackson in early September to roughly 2 points now.
From offense to defense
The clearest sign that the GOP's cash advantage has stalled, however, is where the money is migrating.
In April, the Senate Leadership Fund announced a record $342 million advertising program across eight states designed to protect the GOP majority and expand the map. Texas, Kansas and Nebraska were not among the states.
Since Sept. 1, the SLF and affiliated groups — according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data — have spent or committed roughly $180 million across those three states, all of which Trump carried by double digits in 2024.
"Outside groups are diverting millions into deep-red territory to build defensive moats, leaving pickup opportunities starved for cash in the final stretch," Beckel told CNBC.
But those emergency defenses have come at a cost, diverting money from races Republicans once hoped to win and forcing national groups to narrow the map elsewhere.
In North Carolina, the Senate Leadership Fund initially pledged $71 million to back Republican Michael Whatley. On Oct. 2, however, the group pulled most of its remaining ad reservations after spending about $32.8 million, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, as Democrat Roy Cooper continued to hold a double-digit lead in FiftyPlusOne's polling average.
It's a striking retreat in a perennial battleground where Republicans have won every presidential and Senate election since 2008.
The same triage is unfolding in the House.
The Congressional Leadership Fund cut off spending this week for vulnerable GOP Reps. Thomas Kean Jr. of New Jersey and Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa following grim internal polling. The group also shelved efforts to flip Democratic-held seats represented by Reps. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan and Greg Landsman of Ohio. The spending shifts were first reported by the New York Times.
Those four races had already absorbed about $13.7 million in Congressional Leadership Fund spending through Oct. 14, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. CLF is redirecting roughly $10 million from those races across 16 other districts, according to the Times.
The new spending includes the South Texas seat held by Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, a district Trump carried by 18 points in 2024. De La Cruz herself won reelection by about 14 points in 2024.

articles.title: Huy động hơn 3.500 người từ hơn 40 quốc gia để xây siêu công trình dưới biển dài nhất thế giới, đại gia gốc Thanh Hóa cũng góp mặt
articles.text:
Huy động hơn 3.500 người từ hơn 40 quốc gia để xây siêu công trình dưới biển dài nhất thế giới, đại gia gốc Thanh Hóa cũng góp mặt
Tập đoàn Đại Dũng tham gia cung ứng cấu kiện thép cho tuyến hầm xuyên biển Fehmarnbelt dài 18 km, nối Đan Mạch với Đức.
- 16-10-2026Huy động hơn 11.000 người, đào chuyển 84 triệu mét khối đất để xây siêu sân bay 4,8 tỷ USD, rộng gấp 25 lần Nội Bài, sở hữu kiến trúc có 1-0-2
- 16-10-2026Huy động hơn 104.000 tỷ đồng để xây một nhà ga mới tại siêu sân bay rộng gần gấp 13 lần Nội Bài, tương lai có thể đón 100 triệu khách mỗi năm
Tại eo biển Fehmarnbelt thuộc biển Baltic, tuyến hầm nối đảo Lolland của Đan Mạch với đảo Fehmarn của Đức đang từng bước hình thành. Với chiều dài khoảng 18 km, công trình sẽ trở thành đường hầm chìm dài nhất thế giới khi hoàn thành, phục vụ đồng thời ô tô và tàu hỏa.
Theo Femern Link Contractors (FLC), liên danh phụ trách xây dựng hầm, dự án cần khoảng 3,2 triệu m³ bê tông và 360.000 tấn cốt thép. Riêng lượng cát phục vụ đúc bê tông lên tới khoảng 2 triệu m³.
Điểm khác biệt của Fehmarnbelt nằm ở phương thức thi công. Các đốt hầm được chế tạo tại nhà máy chuyên dụng ven biển Đan Mạch, sau đó vận chuyển nổi ra vị trí lắp đặt và hạ xuống rãnh đào sẵn. Toàn tuyến gồm 79 đốt tiêu chuẩn và 10 đốt đặc biệt, được ghép nối thành đường hầm liên tục dưới biển.
Mỗi đốt tiêu chuẩn dài 217 m, nặng khoảng 73.500 tấn, bố trí các khoang riêng cho đường bộ, đường sắt và hệ thống kỹ thuật. Các đốt đặc biệt có tầng hầm chứa thiết bị điện, được đặt cách nhau khoảng 2 km dọc tuyến.
Để sản xuất những cấu kiện khổng lồ này, công trường vận hành các dây chuyền đúc nối tiếp. Một đốt tiêu chuẩn gồm chín phân đoạn; sau mỗi lần đúc, cấu kiện được đẩy sang vị trí dưỡng hộ để khuôn tiếp tục phục vụ phân đoạn kế tiếp. Theo cập nhật xuân – hè năm 2026 của chủ đầu tư, công trường có hơn 3.500 người đến từ hơn 40 quốc gia làm việc.
Hai cảng công vụ được xây dựng ở hai phía eo biển để phục vụ vận chuyển. Phần lớn vật liệu chế tạo đốt hầm được đưa đến bằng đường thủy. Khi sản xuất đạt cao điểm, lượng đá, xi măng, cát, sỏi và thép được tiếp nhận, xử lý lên tới khoảng 65.000 tấn mỗi tuần.
Ngoài biển, thách thức lớn là vận chuyển và đặt chính xác từng đốt hầm nặng hàng chục nghìn tấn. Hai đầu cấu kiện được bịt kín, giữ không khí bên trong để tạo sức nổi; các khoang nước tạm thời giúp duy trì cân bằng trong quá trình hạ chìm.
Ngày 4/5/2026, đốt đầu tiên rời cảng nhà máy tại Rødbyhavn, được năm tàu kéo cùng thiết bị chuyên dụng IVY đưa tới vị trí lắp đặt. Trước đó, nhà thầu bổ sung khoảng 4.500 tấn bê tông đối trọng để phục vụ quá trình hạ chìm có kiểm soát.
Ngày 7/5, chủ đầu tư thông báo đốt hầm đầu tiên đã được đặt thành công xuống rãnh. Riêng thao tác hạ chìm kéo dài khoảng 14 giờ. Cấu kiện sau đó được kết nối với cửa hầm phía Đan Mạch bằng hệ thống tay đẩy thủy lực, kiểm tra vị trí bằng phép đo laser và bổ sung đá, sỏi dọc hai bên để giữ ổn định.
Trong cập nhật ngày 11/9/2026, chủ đầu tư cho biết ba đốt hầm đã được hạ xuống rãnh. Hệ thống IVY cũng hoàn thành thử tải quan trọng để chuẩn bị lắp đặt các đốt đặc biệt có tầng hầm kỹ thuật, với kích thước dài 39 m, rộng 47 m và cao 13 m.
Để chuẩn bị mặt bằng dưới biển, dự án đã đào khoảng 15 triệu m³ đất, cát và đá. Rãnh đặt hầm có chiều sâu trung bình khoảng 12 m, rộng trung bình khoảng 100 m. Sau khi lắp đặt, các đốt được cố định bằng vật liệu lấp và phủ lớp đá bảo vệ phía trên.
Dù đạt những cột mốc kỹ thuật quan trọng, dự án đã thay đổi tiến độ so với kế hoạch ban đầu. Trong thông báo ngày 17/5/2026, Sund & Bælt cho biết đang xây dựng phương án khai thác hai giai đoạn: đường bộ mở trước, đường sắt vận hành sau khi hạ tầng kết nối cần thiết phía Đức hoàn thành.
Theo đơn vị này, những khó khăn liên quan đến thiết bị hạ chìm chuyên dụng khiến thi công phía Đan Mạch chậm khoảng hai năm. Các giới hạn về tiếng ồn dưới nước, khu vực và thời điểm được phép thi công trong vùng biển Đức cũng ảnh hưởng khả năng bù tiến độ. Vì vậy, mốc mở cửa năm 2029 không còn phù hợp; lịch mới sẽ được xác lập trên cơ sở kinh nghiệm lắp đặt thực tế.
Với tổng vốn đầu tư khoảng 8 tỷ USD (hơn 200.000 tỷ đồng), đây là một trong những dự án hạ tầng giao thông được xem là tham vọng nhất châu Âu, được kỳ vọng sẽ tái định hình mạng lưới vận tải giữa Scandinavia và Trung Âu, đồng thời trở thành mắt xích quan trọng của hành lang giao thông xuyên châu Âu (TEN-T).
Khi được khai thác đồng bộ, tuyến hầm dự kiến rút ngắn thời gian vượt eo biển bằng ô tô từ khoảng 45 phút đi phà xuống còn 10 phút, trong khi tàu hỏa mất khoảng 7 phút. Hành trình đường sắt Copenhagen – Hamburg được kỳ vọng giảm từ gần 5 giờ xuống khoảng 2,5 giờ.
Đáng chú ý, chuỗi cung ứng phục vụ Fehmarnbelt có sự tham gia của Tập đoàn Đại Dũng, doanh nghiệp Việt Nam hoạt động trong lĩnh vực cơ khí chế tạo và kết cấu thép. Theo thông tin doanh nghiệp công bố, Đại Dũng cung ứng các cấu kiện thép quan trọng cho dự án, đáp ứng tiêu chuẩn châu Âu.
Công trình bổ sung một dự án hạ tầng xuyên biển quy mô lớn vào danh mục quốc tế của Đại Dũng, bên cạnh sân vận động Lusail tại Qatar và bảo tàng Powerhouse Parramatta tại Australia,...
Tại Việt Nam, doanh nghiệp là đơn vị thi công mái thép Trung tâm Hội nghị APEC. Công trình có tổng diện tích sàn 157.375 m², gồm 4 tầng nổi và 1 tầng hầm, tích hợp các chức năng hội nghị, triển lãm, tiệc và biểu diễn. Điểm nhấn là không gian hội nghị, triển lãm vượt nhịp 81 m không cột, được kỳ vọng vượt Caesars Forum tại Las Vegas về quy mô ballroom.
Trung tâm có sức chứa tới 10.000 người, bố trí ballroom 3.000 m², hơn 30 phòng họp, trung tâm báo chí phục vụ 3.000–4.000 phóng viên và khu dinner show 2.000 chỗ. Hệ mái sử dụng khoảng 12.000 tấn kết cấu thép, dài hơn 300 m, rộng 165 m, cao 40 m, gồm 13 nhịp chính; nhịp nặng nhất lên tới 722 tấn.
Đại Dũng cũng là đơn vị thực hiện mái vòm thép khổng lồ nặng tới 24.000 tấn tại Trung tâm Hội chợ Triển lãm Quốc gia. Công trình này có tổng diện tích gần 105.000 m2 (tương đương khoảng 10,5 ha), chiều cao đỉnh mái đạt 57 m, hiện được xem là mái vòm lớn nhất hành tinh.
Năm 2026, doanh nghiệp tham gia thi công kết cấu thép sân vận động PVF tại Hưng Yên, nhận thông báo trúng thầu sân vận động VinFast Trống Đồng, đồng thời triển khai các gói thầu tại cầu An Biên và sân bay Quảng Trị.
Trong lĩnh vực công nghiệp – năng lượng, Đại Dũng gia công kết cấu thép cho nhà máy điện khí chu trình hỗn hợp 120 MW, triển khai thỏa thuận sản xuất cẩu cảng STS, RTG cùng các hợp đồng trạm biến áp và đường dây 110 kV tại miền Tây, miền Nam.
Doanh nghiệp đặt mục tiêu doanh thu 12.000 tỷ đồng năm 2026 và đạt mốc 1 tỷ USD trước năm 2030, đồng thời hoàn thiện mô hình tập đoàn với 6 lĩnh vực chuyên sâu, mở rộng sự tham gia vào chuỗi giá trị công nghiệp, hạ tầng trong và ngoài nước.
Việt Nam hàng ngày

articles.title: The affordability crisis isn't hitting all voters equally. Here's why
articles.text:
Affordability is a major theme of the upcoming midterm elections — one that could have implications for how people vote in November.
But not all households are feeling the financial strain equally, according to economists and political experts.
Specifically, older Americans are more insulated from the affordability crunch than younger households such as millennials, the experts said.
"Affordability is the central issue in the forthcoming midterm elections," said William Galston, a senior fellow and chair of governance studies at the Brookings Institution, a think tank. "Nothing else is close."
"Who's feeling these pressures the least? Seniors," he said.
Why seniors are 'doing pretty well'
This isn't to say that older Americans — generally, those age 65 and older — aren't feeling any financial pressures.
They're certainly paying more for food, gasoline, electricity and other items like everybody else amid stubbornly high inflation, economists said.
It's also not to say that all young households find life to be more unaffordable.
However, in aggregate, seniors disproportionately own their homes and are less likely to be first-time homebuyers — meaning they're less exposed to fast-rising mortgage rates and home prices, economists said. They generally drive fewer miles and keep their cars longer — making them less sensitive to high gasoline prices and rising bond yields, which have put upward pressure on auto loan rates, economists said.
Most also don't need childcare, a category that has seen prices soar in recent years, economists said.
And an important chunk of retirees' income — Social Security — is protected from inflation via cost-of-living adjustments, they said. The Social Security Administration on Wednesday announced a 3.6% boost to benefits for 2027, a larger-than-average COLA increase.
"You put it all together, and I would say that — especially if you're 75 and above — you're doing pretty well compared to the rest of America," Galston said. "And the people who are feeling the most pressure are young families in the 30- to 45-year-old range."
Young people are more 'disillusioned'
Financial data supports this generational divide.
Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's, conducted an analysis for CNBC that shows that baby boomers — which Moody's defines as those born between 1946 and 1964 — along with the Silent Generation and older — which it defines as those born in 1945 or earlier — experienced the lowest increase in consumer prices from January 2019 through August 2026.
Zandi used Bureau of Labor Statistics data to generate a weighted consumer price index by generation.
Those two oldest cohorts saw a roughly 31.5% cumulative percent change in consumer prices over that time period, Zandi found.
Meanwhile, millennials — which Moody's defines as those born between 1981 and 1996 — saw the highest cumulative price growth relative to other groups — nearly 2 percentage points higher than that of the older cohorts, at 33.3%. Generation Z, the youngest adult group, born in 1997 or later, had the second-highest rate, at 32.7%.
"Young people are definitely suffering higher rates of inflation than older Americans," Zandi said. "That comes through loud and clear in the data."
"Younger Americans are arguably most disillusioned as they are facing the highest inflation, and thus may turn out to vote to a greater degree," a dynamic that should favor Democrats, he said.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published last week found 78% of Americans said the White House shares blame for higher costs. That includes 64% of Republicans, 76% of independents and 95% of Democrats, according to the poll, which surveyed 4,506 U.S. adults and had a margin of error of plus or minus 1.5 percentage points.
"I think it's fair to say when people are feeling pinched, they look for somebody in leadership to come to them with a solution," said Michael Reid, head of U.S. economics at the Royal Bank of Canada. "I think you'll see some voters turn out and look for whoever is not currently in office as a solution."
Projections indicate Republicans are on track to lose their majority in the House of Representatives in the upcoming midterms, and the Senate majority is "squarely in Democrats' sights," according to the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, which provides nonpartisan analysis of elections and campaigns.
White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton told CNBC in an e-mail that President Donald Trump has delivered "tangible wins" to Americans, including signing a large tax-cut package, which reduced taxes for retirees and workers who get tips and overtime pay, among other things.
Trump is also "delivering on his promise" to stop inflation, raise economic growth and create jobs, "and there will be more to come in the next two years," he wrote.
Housing costs squeeze younger Americans
Younger people spend more of their budgets on housing, which largely accounts for the generational divide in affordability, Zandi said.
Data shows that housing has become increasingly less affordable over the years.
In 2025, the monthly required payment for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was about 33% of the median family's income, an all-time high, up from 26% in 2022, according to the Federal Reserve's report on its Survey of Consumer Finances, published last week.
This 7 percentage point increase was largely driven by rising interest rates and partly by higher house prices, according to the report, which the Fed issues every three years.
Average rates for a 30-year fixed mortgage were 7.4% the week of Oct. 15, according to Freddie Mac data. That's the highest in about three years — since November 2023 — and up from about 6.3% a year ago. Outside of the post-pandemic period, average mortgage rates haven't been this high since 2000, according to Freddie Mac data.
Meanwhile, home prices have outpaced wage gains by a wide margin.
Between 2019 and 2024, the inflation-adjusted median home value increased 30%, from $269,600 to $350,000, according to the Pew Research Center, a nonpartisan, nonprofit research group. The inflation-adjusted median household income for households headed by those under 40 rose only 9% — from $92,700 to $100,900 — during that time, it found.
The only other time the price-to-income ratio for people under 40 reached its current level was during the housing bubble of the mid-2000s, Pew said.
Childcare adds to the affordability crunch
Childcare costs have also risen "substantially faster" than the overall inflation rate, said Galston, at the Brookings Institution.
A Bank of America Institute report published in October 2025 found that childcare expenses are rising 1.5 times faster than the overall U.S. inflation rate.
Families spend about 9% to 16% of their median annual income on full-day care for just one child, and in some cases that cost exceeds their annual rent, according to a 2024 Labor Department report.
Some households can substitute cheaper items for more expensive ones — such as buying chicken instead of beef, for example — as an anti-inflation strategy, Galston said. But it's not really possible to dodge those expenses for families looking for a house or childcare, he said.
Young Americans lose wealth as older households gain
Meanwhile, wealth declined "substantially" for the youngest families from 2022 to 2025, while it soared for older households, according to the Fed's Survey of Consumer Finances.
Families headed by those younger than 35 saw their median net worth fall 23% to $33,000, while families headed by those 75 and older saw it rise 37% to about $505,000, the survey found.
Stocks have posted double-digit annual returns since 2023, largely on the back of euphoria over artificial intelligence, and stocks are assets that tend to be concentrated among older households.
The rise in net worth for the oldest age group is "so large relative to younger age groups" that their net worth exceeded that of families who were nearly or recently retired — in contrast with the previous few survey years, according to the Fed.
Older households can leverage the increase in their wealth to support spending, said Reid, at the Royal Bank of Canada.
A JPMorganChase Institute report published in September shows they are doing exactly that. More than 37% of wealthy retirees — people age 65 or older in the top 10% income group — made net withdrawals from their investment accounts in 2025 to support their spending, up from 24.5% in 2019, according to the report, which examined more than 20 million anonymous Chase checking accounts. Those withdrawals accounted for about 15% of retirees' spending, up from 8% in 2019.
"Certainly the younger generations look worse off in terms of net wealth," he said. "Younger households either have to take on more debt to keep their budget or lifestyle the same, or cut back somewhere. And I don't think older households are having to make that choice yet, in aggregate."
Safety net advantage for older Americans
Of course, seniors tend to spend more of their income on healthcare relative to younger generations, economists said.
"They are burdened by much higher costs for medical care and long-term care," said Jonathan Oberlander, a professor of health policy and political science at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. "And the premium for Medicare Part B — which covers physician visits and other outpatient services — has grown substantially during recent years."
Medicare premiums are expected to rise to $209.50 per month for Part B in 2027, up more than 3% from $202.90 in 2026, according to the Medicare Board of Trustees annual report.
Many workers may face a premium increase in 2027 larger than that of Medicare for employer-sponsored health coverage and health insurance bought on the Affordable Care Act marketplace.
The U.S. social safety net is also broadly "tilted" toward seniors, giving them a big affordability advantage over younger cohorts, said Galston.
Aside from inflation adjustments to Social Security income, older adults who require long-term care have Medicaid as a last-resort backstop in case their financial assets are depleted, he said.
"There, again, there's a safety net," he said. "It's not as though you'll be out on the street."

articles.title: Hà Nội dự kiến bắn pháo hoa tầm cao trong Ngày Văn hóa Việt Nam 24/11
articles.text:
Hà Nội dự kiến bắn pháo hoa tầm cao trong Ngày Văn hóa Việt Nam 24/11
Hà Nội dự kiến tổ chức bắn pháo hoa tầm cao trong 15 phút, kết hợp với chương trình nghệ thuật để phục vụ người dân dịp chào mừng Ngày Văn hóa Việt Nam.
- 16-10-2026Hà Nội chi trả đền bù mở rộng Quốc lộ 1A
- 16-10-2026Đủ 'chiêu trò' trục lợi nhà ở xã hội: Từ thu tiền chênh đến lừa bán 'suất ngoại giao'
- 16-10-2026Những tuyến phố nhiều hoa sữa nhất Hà Nội: Cùng một đoạn đường người đứng lại hít hà, người đeo 2 lớp khẩu trang phóng cho nhanh
UBND TP Hà Nội dự kiến tổ chức chương trình nghệ thuật đặc biệt chào mừng Ngày Văn hóa Việt Nam năm 2026, góp phần đưa Nghị quyết 80 của Bộ Chính trị về phát triển văn hóa Việt Nam và Chỉ thị 35 của Thủ tướng về tổ chức Ngày Văn hóa Việt Nam gắn với Ngày hội Đại đoàn kết toàn dân tộc vào thực tiễn.
Theo kế hoạch, chương trình có thời lượng 120 đến 150 phút, được truyền hình trực tiếp trên kênh H1 của Cơ quan Báo và Phát thanh, Truyền hình Hà Nội; Đài Truyền hình Việt Nam tổ chức tiếp sóng và truyền hình trực tiếp sự kiện trên các kênh, nền tảng của Đài.
Nội dung chương trình được xây dựng theo mạch xuyên suốt, kết nối di sản truyền thống với sáng tạo đương đại, kết hợp nghệ thuật dân tộc với công nghệ sân khấu hiện đại. Qua đó, tạo nên không gian nghệ thuật giàu bản sắc, có chiều sâu tư tưởng và sức lan tỏa xã hội.
Một trong những điểm nhấn của sự kiện là màn pháo hoa tầm cao chào mừng Ngày Văn hóa Việt Nam 24/11, dự kiến kéo dài 15 phút.
Phát biểu tại cuộc họp ngày 15/10, Phó Trưởng ban Tuyên giáo Trung ương, Tổng Biên tập Báo Nhân Dân Lê Quốc Minh nêu quan điểm, chương trình không chạy theo số lượng mà đặt mục tiêu an toàn lên hàng đầu. Số lượng khán giả tập trung trực tiếp trong sân vận động Quốc gia Mỹ Đình dự kiến dưới 40.000 người, nếu tính cả dòng người theo dõi sự kiện ở phía bên ngoài sân qua màn hình LED, chương trình có thể tiếp cận khoảng 100.000 người. Quy mô này được đánh giá phù hợp với không gian sân khấu, đồng thời bảo đảm tính trang trọng của sự kiện.
Ngoài ra, ông Lê Quốc Minh cũng lưu ý cần có các phương án tối ưu nhằm bảo đảm an ninh, an toàn cho khán giả. Về chương trình nghệ thuật, kịch bản cần được nghiên cứu kỹ để bám sát chỉ đạo, đồng thời mang đến hiệu ứng hấp dẫn cho khán giả.
Kết luận tại cuộc họp, Phó Chủ tịch UBND TP Hà Nội Vũ Thu Hà cho biết, thành phố Hà Nội được giao chịu trách nhiệm chính về chương trình nghệ thuật chào mừng Ngày Văn hóa Việt Nam. Đây là chương trình mang tính quốc gia, vì thế thành phố yêu cầu các khâu chuẩn bị phải được thực hiện chỉn chu, cẩn thận, bảo đảm chương trình diễn ra hấp dẫn, thu hút, chất lượng và an toàn tuyệt đối.
Bà Vũ Thu Hà đề nghị các đơn vị được phân công nhanh chóng hoàn tất kịch bản chương trình; thống nhất số lượng người tham gia; xác định vị trí lắp đặt một số màn hình LED ngoài trời để phục vụ người dân theo dõi trực tiếp, đồng thời mở rộng không gian thưởng thức nghệ thuật và tạo sức lan tỏa trong cộng đồng.
Bên cạnh đó, Phó Chủ tịch UBND thành phố lưu ý, màn bắn pháo hoa phải được gắn với kịch bản nghệ thuật để tạo cảm xúc bùng nổ cho khán giả. Các đơn vị chuyên môn cần sớm tiến hành khảo sát thực địa để thống nhất vị trí trận địa pháo hoa, đáp ứng tốt nhất yêu cầu nghệ thuật và an toàn.

articles.title: Schwab to create 'tax-aware' strategy that's been attracting billions from wealthy investors
articles.text:
When Charles Schwab released its quarterly earnings on Thursday, it wasn't the quarterly earnings per share print in the numbers that caught the attention of those who manage money for wealthy stock investors — it was a $60.7 billion figure. That was reported in a detail about margin loan balances which increased 14% quarter-over-quarter to $187.9 billion, including a whopping $60.7 billion related to what are known as "tax-aware" long/short strategies used by many registered investment advisors.
These strategies have been booming as a way for the wealthy to super-charge tax-loss harvesting approaches to stock gains and losses. According to one estimated provided by Tax Alpha Insider to CNBC in September, total assets in TALS surged to more than $170 billion this year from $2 billion in 2022.
Now Schwab is planning to take a bigger piece of that action. On the earnings call, Schwab CEO Rick Wurster said in response to a question from UBS analyst Mike Brown that the broker will launch its own version of the tax-aware long-short strategy.
"Obviously, the tax advantage long/short products have been a meaningful driver of client demand and asset gathering across the industry. There is an increasing number of funds coming to market, and so given Schwab's positioning and client interest in the category, do you see an opportunity to launch a proprietary solution?" Brown asked.
What Schwab's CEO said
"I do expect us to have an offering," Wurster said. "We already have a great direct indexing capability today that has had wonderful performance in terms of tax alpha and delivering for clients, and I expect us to be able to deliver an extended version of that on long/short. ... Certainly another way we can deliver monetization, but more importantly, it is a way we can deliver sustainable long/short strategies to our clients in a way that is operationally and financially manageable over the longer term," Wurster said.
With the stock market posting big gains for multiple years in a row, the wealthy are looking for more ways to shield capital gains from taxes, according to a recent report from CNBC Inside Wealth's Robert Frank. The situation is similar for business owners cashing out and executives with hefty stock compensation packages, and for employees at firms that have gone public in recent years. For the brokers and investment advisors, the products offer relatively high fees and attract new wealthy clients.
How these capital gains tax strategies work
Wealthy investors already use direct indexing strategies on platforms including Schwab to pair up stock gains and losses in a tax efficient way. The issue that wealthy investors run into with standard tax-loss harvesting is that fewer and fewer losses become available to harvest over time, according to an overview of TALS from advisor research platform Kitces. "Because on average, the market tends to rise, and so in a diversified portfolio most positions will eventually rise far enough above their cost basis that even subsequent downturns don't result in taxable losses, while for positions that do continue to decline there's only a finite amount of losses they can actually generate (because their market value – and cost basis – can only go down to zero)," it wrote.
Tax-aware long-short strategies get around this by adding leverage on both the long and short side of an existing portfolio, with the investor buying more positions and increasing the number of potential losses to harvest. That allows the portfolio to remain "economically neutral ... And because short positions can theoretically generate an infinite amount of losses (since they decline when markets rise), TALS portfolios are less likely to run out of losses to harvest over time than standard long-only portfolios," Kitces noted.
Questions remain, from access to tax risks
Brent Sullivan of Tax Alpha Insider noted in a post on X on Thursday that advisors will have many questions about the Schwab products, which he noted should not be referred to as "funds" — UBS analyst Brown used that terminology in his question. Sullivan wrote that it is reasonable to speculate that a Schwab product could "meaningfully lower" the assets under management minimum requirement typical on these products, but it is also an open question as to whether the products will only be available to Schwab advisers and only on Schwab's platform.
Wurster provided few details, and no timeline for a launch. "We are thrilled about that, working on it, and we will give more updates in future calls as to when that may launch," he said.
The government has been taking a more aggressive stance on tax avoidance strategies and some though not all "tax alpha" strategies of the wealthy, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the IRS recently issuing a notice over the use of sophisticated ETF strategies to shield capital gains from taxation. The notice also expressed interest in "tax-aware" strategies typically structured as partnerships or separately managed accounts, but according to an analysis from law firm Ropes & Gray, it also made clear that "tax-aware" itself is not a cause for concern and year-end tax loss harvesting is a well-established practice.

articles.title: U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says
articles.text:
BANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market access issues for Mastercard Inc and Citigroup Inc during at least two bilateral meetings with Chinese counterparts in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official.
The Treasury delegation, led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke, held bilateral meetings with officials from the People's Bank of China and the finance ministry on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance meetings and the IMF-World Bank annual gathering this week, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door meetings.
The talks included market access for U.S. companies, including Mastercard, Visa and Citigroup, the official said, adding that regulatory approval was part of the agreement reached during the meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping during the latter's state visit in Washington last month.
The sideline meetings in Bangkok continued discussions on implementing these deals, the official said.
The PBOC, China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, China Securities Regulatory Commission, Chinese embassies in Singapore and Thailand, the U.S. Treasury Department press office and Visa did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Citigroup and Mastercard declined to comment.
The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa Inc. to begin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business. Visa has up to a year to prepare before it applies for an operating license, the PBOC has said.
China has opened much of its financial sector to foreign firms since 2018, gradually lifting foreign ownership caps on services such as securities, futures and fund management. It still limits cross-border capital flows and has kept state-backed domestic players dominant in payments.
Mastercard currently operates yuan card payments in China through a local joint venture with NetsUnion Clearing Corp., which began operating in 2024. The pending approval would allow it to operate as an independent entity, the person said.
Citigroup — which has hired several dozen employees for its China unit — is seeking a wholly owned securities license to conduct A-share brokerage, underwriting, research and principal trading businesses in the onshore market, two people familiar with the industry said, requesting anonymity for discussing private matters.
One of the two people close to Citigroup said the bank planned to increase its China securities staff to about 100.
The bank applied in late 2021, and Reuters reported last month that approval could come soon.
Trump and Xi are expected to meet in person for the third time this year in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November.
"The move suggests the US-China trade environment remains benign, and Beijing is keen to keep up the momentum," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group.
Licensing U.S. financial firms is a "limited concession" on market access, she said, though it signals China is continuing to open up, and "this should marginally bolster investor confidence in Chinese assets."

articles.title: Công an bất ngờ kiểm tra cửa hàng Dương Dolce, khởi tố Nguyễn Văn Dương SN 2000
articles.text:
Công an bất ngờ kiểm tra cửa hàng Dương Dolce, khởi tố Nguyễn Văn Dương SN 2000
Nguyễn Văn Dương bị khởi tố về tội “Xâm phạm quyền sở hữu công nghiệp".
- 24-08-2026Kiểm tra cửa hàng đồng hồ, khởi tố ông chủ Nguyễn An Bình SN 1990
- 14-10-2026Phó Tổng giám đốc một doanh nghiệp trên sàn bị khởi tố vì trộm cắp tài sản
- 01-10-2026Khởi tố 9 bị can, thu hồi hơn 118 tỷ đồng trong vụ Công ty Việt Mỹ
Ngày 16/10/2026, Công an tỉnh Hưng Yên cho biết, ngày 21/9/2026, Công an xã Hưng Hà, tỉnh Hưng Yên phối hợp với Đội Quản lý thị trường số 6, Chi cục Quản lý thị trường tỉnh Hưng Yên tiến hành kiểm tra cửa hàng Dương Dolce, địa chỉ tại thôn Thanh Tân, xã Hưng Hà, tỉnh Hưng Yên, do Nguyễn Văn Dương, sinh năm 2000, trú tại thôn Chi Lăng, xã Thần Khê, tỉnh Hưng Yên làm chủ hộ kinh doanh.
Qua kiểm tra, lực lượng chức năng phát hiện hộ kinh doanh đang trưng bày để bán số lượng lớn hàng hóa có dấu hiệu giả mạo nhãn hiệu, gồm: 270 đôi dép giả nhãn hiệu HERMÈS; 12 đôi giày giả nhãn hiệu DIOR; 08 đôi giày giả nhãn hiệu GUCCI và 125 bộ quần áo giả nhãn hiệu adidas. Tổng giá trị hàng hóa theo giá niêm yết là 222.600.000 đồng.
Trên cơ sở kết quả kiểm tra, ngày 28/9/2026, Đội Quản lý thị trường số 6, Chi cục Quản lý thị trường tỉnh Hưng Yên đã ban hành Quyết định về việc chuyển hồ sơ vụ vi phạm có dấu hiệu tội phạm, đồng thời chuyển toàn bộ hồ sơ và tang vật có liên quan đến Cơ quan Cảnh sát điều tra Công an tỉnh Hưng Yên để xem xét, xử lý theo quy định của pháp luật.
Căn cứ tài liệu, chứng cứ thu thập, ngày 14/10/2026, Cơ quan Cảnh sát điều tra Công an tỉnh ra Quyết định khởi tố vụ án, khởi tố bị can đối với Nguyễn Văn Dương về tội “Xâm phạm quyền sở hữu công nghiệp”, quy định tại khoản 1 Điều 226 Bộ luật Hình sự. Hiện cơ quan Công an đang tiếp tục củng cố hồ sơ xử lý đối tượng theo quy định của pháp luật.
Một số hình ảnh tang vật của vụ án:
Vụ việc là lời cảnh báo đối với các tổ chức, cá nhân hoạt động kinh doanh trong việc chấp hành nghiêm các quy định của pháp luật về sở hữu trí tuệ, nguồn gốc, xuất xứ hàng hóa và bảo vệ quyền lợi người tiêu dùng. Việc kinh doanh, buôn bán hàng hóa giả mạo nhãn hiệu không chỉ xâm phạm quyền và lợi ích hợp pháp của chủ sở hữu nhãn hiệu mà còn tiềm ẩn nguy cơ gây thiệt hại cho người tiêu dùng, ảnh hưởng đến môi trường kinh doanh lành mạnh.
Thời gian tới, Công an xã Hưng Hà tiếp tục phối hợp với các lực lượng chức năng tăng cường công tác nắm tình hình địa bàn, kiểm tra, phát hiện và xử lý các hành vi vi phạm pháp luật trong hoạt động sản xuất, kinh doanh hàng hóa; đồng thời đẩy mạnh tuyên truyền, vận động các hộ kinh doanh nâng cao ý thức chấp hành pháp luật, không sản xuất, tàng trữ, buôn bán hàng giả, hàng hóa giả mạo nhãn hiệu, góp phần bảo đảm an ninh, trật tự và xây dựng môi trường kinh doanh minh bạch, lành mạnh trên địa bàn.

articles.title: What we want to see when Capital One and Meta report earnings next week
articles.text: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer holds a "Morning Meeting" livestream at 10:20 a.m. ET. Here's a recap of Friday's key moments. 1. Stocks are mixed Friday, with the rotation out of AI names and into defensives still ongoing. The sharp week-to-date losses in the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the weekly gains in the Dow tell the story. Club portfolio director Jeff Marks highlighted the financial sector as an industry benefiting from the market shift after a rough start earlier this week following earnings. Club banks Wells Fargo , Bank of New York , and Goldman Sachs are all positive for the week. Consumer staples names like Club holding Kimberly-Clark extended gains, after seeing one of its best days in years Thursday. We just put out a commentary on all the things going right for the consumer products giant and a major catalyst ahead. 2. Apple shares are modestly higher, tracking to eclipse Wednesday's record-high close, as preorders kicked off Friday for the company's highly anticipated iPhone Duo. Apple's first foldable iPhone will hit stores next on Oct. 23. Early indications suggest demand is already strong. Jeff pointed to delivery estimates pushing into early 2027 as an encouraging signal. “That is a very good sign, especially because these phones come with a very high price point,” Jeff said, referencing the Duo's starting price of $1,999. Jim Cramer has been bullish on the Duo since getting a first look at the device at Apple's flagship store in New York in September. “When I experimented with this two-sided seamless phone … I was blown away,” Jim said during Thursday's October Monthly Meeting , adding that he plans to get the Duo as a second phone. 3. Club name Capital One is set to report earnings Tuesday evening. Jeff said the key issue for the bank and credit card provider is how much it continues to invest in its business, as that spending has weighed on profits. "Investors typically don't want to hear about investment years. They want profit," Jeff said. "That is part of the reason why the stock has struggled this year," he added, referencing Capital One's over 16% year-to-date decline. Meta Platforms , also a portfolio name, reports its quarterly results after Wednesday's close. "We know the Muse personal AI agent has been a hit," Jeff said. "Now, I think the question is how much investment comes with that." The potential for increased spending was one reason we trimmed our Meta position to protect profits last month. The stock, which surged in the two weeks after the Muse launch on Sept. 8, has cooled off a bit recently. With the company expected to deploy tons of cash toward expanding Muse, investors will be closely watching its capital expenditure plans.
